div.p: McDOUGALL'S Paterit SELF—RAISING FLOUR eINvEA;L'I&I.
(Copyright.)

be shot) and Dudley Thotpe's hat which had a bullet-hole through it. There was a suspicion of swagger about Dudley that day; no longer was he An untried recruit, but a soldier who had been under fire and nree inches off death. The Australians sighed for a closer introduction to the enemy. Bitterly did they criticise the Boers' tactics.

"You'll have a bellyful of fighting soon," an old soldier promised them, "and be in warmer places than you like. This war is going to be a big thing. We were going to advance weeks ago, and we daren't leave our base."

The prophecy came true ; the next day a scout rode into camp with loose rein, and a horse that could only stand and gasp when he pulled up and jumped from the saddle. "They're at Straker's Farm," he cried to those surrounding him, as he hurried to report himself, and the word passed from mouth to mouth. Straker's Farm was twelve miles to the east, owned by loyalists, and no move- ment of the enemy had previously been reported in that quarter. Within an hour two hundred mounted men were in the saddle and riding eastward. Bond and Thorpe grinned with joy at each other. "This is my birthday," whispered the latter, "my birthday party; ain't I going to enjoy it!" Alas, for Dudley! His rejoicings were pre- mature. True was it the Boer laager was dis- covered, and a pretty little fight ensued in which the Australians greatly dittinguished themselves, manceuvring the enemy out of their positions and putting them to flight, but Dudley took no part in it all. Almost as soon as his troops opened fire, a bullet took him in the thigh, and, reeling in the saddle with agony, he fell a minute later from his horse. John Bond picked him up, and, dragging him to the shelter of a rock, poured some of the contents of a flask between his white lips. Dudley revived. "I'm all right," he gasped. "Don't—don't lose the fun for me."

Hours passed, and he lay there listening to the distant fusillade, groaning with pain, half delirious; his leg throbbed and throbbed; he wondered vaguely whether he would lose it, and was almost unconscious when the doctor found him. Four of his comrades laid him on an improvised stretcher and bore him to the farm, and of what happeneej after the wounded man had no knowledge at all. '

' He awoke to find himself in a comfortable bed in a pretty, tiny ,square room, a girl sitting near knitting. Dudley felt stiff and sore, unable to move a finger. He looked at the girl. "They haven't cut my leg off, have they ? " he whispered. "No, no," she reassured him. "It's only a bad flesh wound; you'll be all right in a few days."

She gave him some broth, and he smiled at her and fell asleep again. When he next woke he felt much stronger and better; this time, besides the girl, there was an elderly lady in the room. She told the sick man he was at Straker's Farm, the doctor thinking it better to leave him there than risk the long journey in his present condition. -- "I'm afraid I'm giving you a lot of trouble." She emphatically denied it. "The least we women can do is to tend the wounded among the brave men who protect us. And in your case there is a special reason. Your friend said your name is Dudley Thorpe. Are you not a son of Dudley Thorpe, the old squire a Gillington Hall, in Sussex.? "
"Why, you're Mrs. Heron," he cried, with a flash of recollection. "You," he added, to the girl, "must be Juliet."

- "I'm glad you remember me," and her blue eyes smiled a friendly welcome to her old acquaintance. Colonel Heron, Dudley leprnt, was dead, and two years before Mrs. Heron, somewhat alarmed about her daughter,iwho seemed predisposed to consump- tion, had coil° to Africa to stay with her two bachelor brothers, the Strakers of Straker's Farm. The fine air of the colony had cured Juliet, and they had stayed. Mrs. Heron went on to tell that upon the outbreak of war (which had not been expected) her brothers had been obliged to leave the farm to avoid being commandeered. She and Juliet had declined to fly; they had been on good terms with their Dutch neighbours, and remained to protect the Strakers' property. Her brothers had enlisted in the Colonial Horse. Two days later Dudley was up and able to hobble with the aid of two sticks; the Herons made much of him, and the old feud was forgotten, or, at least, never mentioned. A week followed, during which the inmates of the farm heard no news of the outside world except a preposterous rumour that the British camp had been shifted further south. , This news came from a Mar. "Of course, it's not true," said Dudley; "but it's funny they don't come this way." He sat smoking on the stoop one afternoon when Juliet, who had gone out to feed the poultry, rushed back. "The Boers are coming," she panted, "and -that hateful Van Riet 0 Dudley, I wonder if they'll take you away as a prisoner? Lie down on the sofa and pretend you can't walk."

"Confound their cheek!" grumbled Dudley. obeying. "Who's Van Riet, Juliet?" "You'll know directly," she said, grimacing. "Don't offend him, for goodness' sake!" Three horsemen cantered up, and the leader took off his hat. "Welcome, Mees Juliet," he cried. "Some Cape brandy, if you please, to drink to your beautiful eyes, as your poet says. Who the deuce is this man?" he concluded, abruptly. Juliet briefly explained. "Alit An Australian! Well, you may stop here till your leg is well. But, had you been an Afrikander, I'd have carried you off tied to my stirrup! " "Yu temper mercy with justice," acknowledged Thorpe but the .sarcasm missed fire. Van Riet permitted his two men to have a drink and despatched them; he himself sat down in a wicker chair and made himself comfortable.

"Well, we have beaten you again! " he said, genially. "Your General has had to shift his camp; they are twenty-five miles away from you now. Yes, it is the truth I tell. Ladysmith also has fallen—at least, it will fall this week, and there is news of European intervention t" The Dutchman was a sturdy, well-built young man, not ill-looking, and apparently well acquainted with the Herons. The farm, he said, was already confiscated. He was the owner. But, worse than all this, he proceeded to make love to Juliet. The girl parried his clumsy advances, declining to take his protestations seriously, and rallying him on a Dutch sweetheart which, she declared, he pos- sessed. Could he deny that he had asked Rosa Mentz to "upsit " with him? He denied it on oath. At last, when the situation for two out of the trio was becoming unbearable, Mrs. Heron appeared, and the visitor became better-mannered. The dignified English lady was obviously feared by him. The scouts at last re-appeared. Van Riet took his departure. Mrs. Heron returned to superintend some kitchen work, and Dudley, left alone with Juliet, broke into a tirade of wrath. It was infamous that she should be subjected to the presence of such a bounder. He would ride to the camp that night (for he did not believe the story of the retreat) and ask for a patrol to protect the farm and its inmates. Juliet made light of the matter.

"I believe you like the fellow's attentions," cried the Australian, wrathfully. "Well, I like your taste. An insufferable cad!" "How dare you insult me You are worse than Van Riet! Can't you see we are all in his power ? " Juliet flung the sentences at him with hot cheeks, and departed, leaving him to his reflections. He had humiliatingly to confess himself in the wrong; but an ample apology next day brought Juliet's forgiveness. They discussed the situation. It was by this time almost certain the British retreat Van Riet had spoken of had taken place; and the inmates of Straker's Farm could not rely on the protection of the' Queen's flag. Van Riet held some sort of commission in the neighbourhood, and could do as he pleased for the time. He had, Juliet confided, been a humble suitor hitherto, and she had never taken him seriously or bestowed two thoughts on him; but the Bo.r successes had wondrously chatted him. "I'm not afraid of him," said Juliet, frankly; '"but I must be civil ..to him at any cost. I really think,. Dudley, as soon as you can sit a horse, you had better try and rejoin the camp. Van Riet may any day take it into his head to send you off to Pretoria."
"And leave you—and Mrs. Heron? " cried Dudley. "But my poor boy, . you can't help us by staying." . _

a ri-u not so sure. Anyway, I shan't budge." A sudden shyness fell upon them. Van Riot had unconsciously pulled a veil from their eyes, and they saw themselves standing on the threshold of the, unknown. Juliet's predicament would have aroused the dhivalrysthe brotherly protection of any Anglo-Saxon ; but as the man was young and heart- whole, and the girl sweet and fair and lovable.

div.head: JULIET OF STRAKER'S FARM.
div.p: JULIET OF STRAKER'S FARM.
By CHARLES D. LESLIE, Author of "The Gold Trap," "The Hamilton Honeymoon," "The Best Man," &e.

Australia—young Australia, stalwart and lusty son of a mother old -in years but vigorous and healthy as her offspring—was bidding farewell to a contingent of troopers bound to South Africa to serve their Queen. It was a memorable day. For awhile Anglo-Saxon phlegm was laid aside. The Governor farewell speech roused enthusiasm to white heat. Bands blared, banners waved, inn shouted themselves hoarse, women's eyes—aye, ak.d men's—were dim with tears. A wave of emotiOn enveloped one and all. The day marked an epoch in the history of the Ocean Continent: a step forward in the history of the mighty British Empire. The young men themselvels, the heroes of the hour, Australia's gift to the Great Queen, the young men—long-limbed, clear-eyed, clean-built, sound as race-horses, and tough as terriers, worthy repre- sentatives of their nation—answered the populace with cheer for cheer; proud men were they that day, and when finally the steamer moved from land and their native continent commenced to dwindle from view, they hung on deck almost in silence watching it, with emotions too deep for words. They felt overpowered by the responsibility imposed upon them, the honour of the flea entrusted to their keeping. Under their breath 'they swore to be worthy of their country's confidence. Never should Australia have cause' to blush for them or call them unworthy sons.

The voyage .was three days old and the men shaking into the routine cf the ship; a group of them were engaged in the popular shipboard pastime of "making their mark." The game is as follows: A chalk line is drawn on the deck, and the com- petitor stands with his toes touching it, and a piece of chalk in his right hand. He drops forward on the deck, resting his weight on the left palm, and, lean- ing as far as he can forward without overbalancing, marks the deck with the chalk in his right hand; he must then, without shifting his left hand, regain his original upright attitude behind the chalk line. If he has thrown himself so far forward that this is impossible unless his knees touch the deck, the mark is rubbed out. He who makes this mark furthest from the chalk line remains the winner. It is obvious length of limb is the chief requisite of success. But not entirely; on this occasion John Bond, the tallest man of the company, standing six feet three inches in his socks, was beaten by Dudley Thorpe, who only measured a poor bare six feet. Bond, a good-natured giant, took his defeat good-humouredly, and thereupon struck up a warm friendship for Thorpe. Both were squatters in New South Wales. Bond had a father living; Thorpe 's had died some years before, and the holding belonged to his three sons, of whom Dudley was the eldest. The latter spoke in admiration of his brothers' attitude: all had wanted to enlist, but the two younger had in the end acknowledged his right to represent the family and their duty to stay on the farm and look after it and, last but not least, their mother.
"Were you born in Australia or at home ? " asked Bond.
He himself was an Australian born, and his father had been forty years in the colony, but En.eand was "home" for all that.

Dudley answered he had been born in Sussex, and was ten years of age when his father 'emigrated, fifteen years before. "We come from Kent," confided John. "I've cousins there now, and an uncle, a parson ;some time I hope to go and see them. I suppose one day you hope to go and look up your relations in Sussex? "

Dudley thought not; there were no Thorpes in Sussex now, though he believed he had distant cousins in the Midlands. His father had been squire and chief land owner in Gillington, near Haselmere ("where Tennyson lived, you know") and generations of Thorpes ,lay buried in the churchyard and in the vault underneath the church. The pride of caste and descent uncon- sciously revealed itself in the democratic young Australian's words. Bond understood these were confidences for his ear alone. He pressed for further information. What had made the squire leave his ancestral home and county? "He ruined himself," confessed Dudley, "over lawsuits and speculations. Our nearest neighbour was a retired soldier, Colonel Heron. He and my father were friends at first, and my mother and Mrs. Heron always got on. I had a sister (she's dead), just the age of Juliet, the Herons' only child, and the maters used to compare babies, and all that. But dad and Heron quarrelled over some- thing or other, and went to law about it, and it proved a very expensive case. By the time it got to the House of Lords, my father had taken to speculating to pay his legal expenses, and that smashed him entirely. He was too proud to live in the parish a poor man instead of a rich one, for we had to turn out of the Hall, and so we all emigrated. I was going to Rugby; I went to Australia instead." "Hard lines," said John ..Bond, sympathetically. "It was my first real grief, and the last time I cried; I was just ten, and when I learnt I wasn't to go to Rugby, I went down to the river and blubbered. Little Juliet found me there L•sbe was about five then—l remember her well, a little dot of a girl in a white frock with yellow ribbons, and kl-mbicd yellow curls over her face. he must have escaped from her nurse and was gathering, flowers. She offered me her mite of a pocket-handkerchief to wipe my eyes, and I made her promise not to tell anyone she'd seen me crying. I was ashamed of myself. Yes," continued Dudley, reflectively, stretching himself in his chair, "I'd like to see Gillington again. If I worry through this campaign, and the Boers don't shoot me, I've half a mind to go straight to England from the Cape, when we are discharged. It's the best chance I'll ever have."

"What! - Not come back with us ? " remonstrated Bond. "Think of the reception we shall have, the ovations, the banquets, and the women all worship- ing us Why, any of us can have the pick of the prettiest girls for the asking, if he wants to marry, especially if he has some honourable scars to shew. Dudley became philosophical rather than enthusiastic at this prospect. "I don't profess to understand women," he confessed ; "they never mean what they say, or say what they mean. The useful ones are always ugly, and the pretty ones think such a lot of themselves. If ever I marry I'll want a wife who's useful and ornamental too. Guess I'll die a bachelor," he concluded, in a tone of gentle resignation.
The psychology of woman as a subject of conver- sation was speedily dropped for the more enthralling one of the coming campaign.

When the steamer dropped anchor in Table Bay —the bay which Afrikanders patriotically vow is far superior to Naples—the Australians paced the deck, eager to be off the ship and at the enemy. They were wanted, they learnt, and need have no fear of coming too late for the fray. No time did they waste gazing at the white houses of the town, at the dark mountain towering skywards, its head swathed in mist; the war wiped the scene from their eyes. They were speedily engaged in rehding newspapers, gathering the latest news. They landed and were royally welcomed, but small time was permitted to enjoy the hospitality of the loyalists; straightway they were entrained and rattled up-country for weary hours and dumped down in a tiny village, the headquarters of a brigade; and almost within touch with the rebel colonists, reinforced by Transvaalers and Free Staters. Khaki-clad men strolled to meet them, giving them greeting, and freely sharing the scanty luxuries procurable. They were provided with mounts good, bad, and indifferent, and toiled from dawn to sunset to become efficient troopers, and fit for duty. Sundry lancers when off duty, watched them critically the while, and announced they would do.

the baptism of fire came a few days later, and proved a very disappointing affair. The only satisfied man was Dudley Thorpe. It befell thus. A party of twenty, reconnoitring to the north of the camp,. unearthed a few Boers among the low- lying hills, and a skirmish at long range ensued. For the first time the Australians knew what it felt like to be shot at. The whiz of the Mauserhullet coming, seemingly, out of nowhere, and plugging the ground about them", sang in their ears. They acquitted themselves well, but the Boers, elusive as ever,. vanished over the hills and into the air, it seemed, and the squadron had nothing to shew for the skirmish hia wouna,ml horse (which had to

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, December 10, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 10, 1904.

love woke as well. Juliet stood a modern Andromeda, and Perseus (of New South Wales) could only curse his impotence to slay the monster and rescue the maiden. He asked nothing more of fate than to get her out of Van Riet's clutches. And afterwards ? Well, who was there like Juliet a the wide wcrld ? Could he but win her favour, her love, here was the wife "both useful sad ornamental" he had been -vaguely and leisursly seeking. But there was little chance of telling her this, for somehow he never found her alone, and the days were very long and dreary, and nothing happened. No news came to them for the space of four days. Night had just fallen, and Dudley sat alone smok- ing on the stoep. Mrs. Heron had retired to bed early with a headache, and Juliet was tending her. Suddenly, out of the darkness, a horseman appeared and Van Riet's voice broke the silence, "Hullo, there! Anyone about ? " Dudley answered. "Ah ! The Australian. , How's your leg? Just hobble, can you ? Got an hour to spare." . . . . He sprang from his horse and came upon the verandah. Dudley, in reply to queries, said he be- lieved Miss Juliet would be down directly. The Dutchman was loquacious and excited.
"How's the war getting on? We don't hear anything," said the Australian.

The great news came out with a burst. What fools the English were! A great disaster was about to overtake them; on the morrow the whole brigade would be dead or prisoners. That night they were about to make a surprise attack on the Boer laager. Through their spies, the latter were fully prepared, and the attacking force would walk into a death-trap. Hardly had the disclosure been made than the Dutchman felt he had been guilty of an indiscre- tion. True, the other man was unarmed and wounded, but—with a premonition of danger—Van Riet rose, drawing his revolver: "Here," he cried, roughly, "come out of the dark there where I can see you."

D-udley obeyed promptly; he sprang at his enemy like a wild cat and pinned Van Riet's arms to his side before he could point the revolver. The Dutchman, though taken by surprise, was the stronger man. But knowledge of what hung on his escape gave Dudley desperate strength. In his mind's eye, he saw the record of the night's work he alone could prevent. "Disaster in Cape Colony," "Defeat and Rout of a Brigade." "Heavy Losses." He twined his arms round Van Riet and strove to overthrow him. There was little sound as the two men struggled on the verandah; they panted behind clenched teeth and strained sinew a.nd muscle. Dudley's barely healed wound broke.

—she was almost upon it bet ore the sudden rear n, might be guarded crossed her mind; it was too late to retreat; in fear and trembling she rode on unchallenged. She gave a sob of relief as she passed through. And now she was surely safe. A very few minutes and she had reached the road and drew rein. Just in time; on her left a faint sound broke the stillness—it grew louder and nearer—the sound of marching men. She advanced, and out of the darkness a swift hand seized her bridle and a dozen rifle barrels were levelled at .her.
"A woman!" cried a voice, in atone of disgust. Khaki-clad soldiers surrounded her, the van- guard of the British column. "I've come to warn you. You're going to your deaths 1"

Somewhat incoherently she poured out her tale; the whole line was checked. A mounted aide rode up swearing softly and demanding cause of delay. Soon the brigadier himself was on the spot and heard her story. "We have our scouts on ahead ? " he asked a subordinate. "Yes, sir; Ferris and Hale." _ _ _ _
"They've probably been captured; send four of the best men forward, MacKenzie; let them keep off the road and reconnoitre with the utmost caution."
A quarter of an hour passed and a scout returned. "Enemy largely ambushed, sir, on the west of the pass." In another five minutes another man appeared.

"Boers in large force east of the maintain, and-" His speech was cut short by a rifle shot from ahead. "That's O'Connor," concluded the man, coolly. "Knew he'd blunder into 'em!" "You are close by the Stein Kopje," said Juliet at this juncture. "It would be an admirable position-" "You've an 'ead on your shoulders, young lady! " observed the scout, admiringly. "That's our best point, sir." As for what followed, is it not written in the history of the war? How the attacking force lay perdu till dawn, and then, issuing from the kopje, fell upon the Boers. Of the execution done by the light artillery guns; of the brilliant work of the Lancers and Australians. In brief, the enemy was driven out of the neighbourhood, and the new camp headquarters pitched 133 J Straker's Farm. Two days later the whole force moved further north. But all this does not concern us.
"Grumble!" cried Dudley Thorpe, again a prisoner in bed. "Haven't I cause to grumble? Here's the doctor saying it's months before I'll be at for service again. And I feel weaker than an infant! "
ungrateful wretch! Am not I going to nurse you? And the brigadier has been saying all see. of nice things about you; you are to be

he felt the throb, and the blood running clown ins leg. He never heeded. Crash! They fell together to the floor, Van Riet undermost. Dudley took his adversary_ by the throat and clung like a bull-dog, 'but he was fint- ing from loss of blood and weakening. He felt sick and weary and tired. Van Riet was shaking his head free, but just then the Australian touched a knife-handle in the other's belt. He drew it, struck once, twice, and saw as in a dream Juliet's face, pale and frightened, by the dim light of a candle. He fainted.

"Why did you do it?" cried the girl, anxiously, when he revived a few minutes later. "Why did you fight Van Riet ? You've nearly killed him." She had piled cushions under Dudley and bound his leg; he lay in a pool of his blood. "'Where is he ? "
"Over there, unconscious; you stabbed him with his own knife."

"Listen, Juliet. Hundred of men's lives depend on you this night. Mount your mare and ride to the British camp at Stelfontein ; they are attacking the Boer laager at Vaalplaat to-night and *alking into a death-trap. They are going through the Two Sisters.' There is an ambuscade there. For God's sake go at once!" Again he fainted. The girl did not hesitate a minute ; she kissed the unconscious DndleY,and left him where he lay. Van Riet's wounds shl had already roughly bandaged; for good or ii he was powerless for many hours to come. Her mother, she knew, was asleep. In five minutes she had saddled her mare. The Kaffir servants were asleep—and, moreover, in such an emergency, she dared trust none of them. The late British reverses had made them utterly unreliable.

" ----- J A ride of twenty miles was before her. She knew the way; by bearing to the right, skirting the eastern Sister (the "Two Sisters " were two tall hills) she would dome out on the Stelfontein road 'below the pass, in time to check the advancing column. Out into the night she rode. I few stars shone overhead and the breeze fanned her burning cheeks. The darkness had no terrors for her she rather welcomed it as hiding her from the enemy. Several miles were quickly passed; and her tumultuous fears were calming, when she rode right into a Boer picket. In a second she was by, and heard shouts and oaths in the rear, then a splutter of fire; but she was too much occupied with her \ horse to be frightened; and the shots were ineffectual. For miles the chase was hot, but her mount was the fresher, and distanced the pursuers. Would she get through? Would she be in time? Inky black against the dark sky she saw the Sister; it was (she calculated roughly), five miles away, —twenty minutes' ride at her present pace. Dead uv an the earth. The Steinfordein Drift

Followed a pause. "I say, Juliet ? " "Yes." "Would you mind very much if—if I did? "I would try and endure it," answered Juliet, meekly. Mrs. Heron was delighted when they told her, Ind the news of the engagement ran through the camp and roused enthusiasm. What made it specially romantic, said the best informed, was that the lady was an heiress—a fact of which Thorpe was ignorant—and the owner of Gillington Hall, in Sussex, the ancestral home of the Thorpes, which Thorpe's father had lost through rash spwulation, anct miss seron's father bought; and the young, couple would go and live there. As for the Australian troopers, they came to the farm before they went north, and, demanding to see the heroine of the night march, the girl whoso pluck had converted a certain disaster into a %riumph, gave, with all the power of their lungs, three hearty British cheers for "Juliet of Straker's Farm."

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
EXTENSIVE SEWERAGE SCHEME. Compensation for a Tram Conductor.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held on Tuesday when there were present, the Mayor (presiding). the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Fairclough), Aldermen A. Bennett, John Evans, R. W. Francomb, T. Huchinson, W. Pierpoint, J. Smethurst, T. H. Sutton; Councillors T. H. Ashcroft, T. Barton, W. Benson' W. Brough, T. Burton, W. Clegg, J. G. Craik, James Evans, L. Ellison, T. J. Hulse, J. Lord, A. Peacock, P. Peacock, J. Pemberton, J. Roberts: J. Sankey, J. Skelland, J. F. Smith, F. Stott, D. Tinmon, J. Wilkinson, W. J. Wilson, T. Wright, Messrs. J. L. Whittle (town clerk), S. Wilson (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasnrer),J. Deas (water engineer), W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), J. G. Gornall (medical officer), J. M. Murray (director of education.) REPRESENTATIVE ON THE EDUCATION

the minutes of the Markets Committee said the com- mittee were considering the question of the police and the protection of the markets, in conjunction with the Watch Committee, and at the nest monthly meetin g they would report what had been done. Councillor ROBERTS seconded, and the motion was carried.

div.head: COMMITTEE.
div.p: COMMITTEE.

Alderman BENNETT proposed the appointment of Mr. Holman Kingdon on the Education Committee (recom- mended by the Chamber of Commerce),in place of'Coun- cillor Fulton Smith. He remarked that Mr. Kingdon had a considerable knowleige of technical and educa- tional matters, and the firm with which he was connec- ted had greatly helped the Education Committee in their work. rflear. hear). Councillor ELLrsoN seconded, and the motion was carried.

div.head: REPRESENTATIVE MANAGER.
div.p: REPRESENTATIVE MANAGER.
Councillor Brough was appointed a representative manager of the Heathside National School, in the place of Mr. Dodds, resigned. SECONDARY AND TECEINICAL EXAMINATIONS.

Alderman BENNETT in proposing the adoption of the minutes of the Education Committee, referred to the published results of the recent examination in the Secondary Schools and Technical Institute which he said showed a very decided improvement, as compared with the previous year. Councillor ELLISON seconded and the minutes were approved.
IS THE PRESENT POLICE FORCE SUFFICIENT,? COUNCIL DECIDE THAT IT IS NOT.

A discussion took place upon the subjeet of increas- ing the numerical strength of the police force, the Watch Committee having recommended the appointment of four additional constables. The committee also resolved that the Electricity and Tramways Committee be requested to allow the police to travel on the tram- cars free when wearing their duty badges. The com- mittee considered the question of watching the markets and it wasegreed that if the Markets Committee will pay the wages of one constable, this committee will undertake to watch the markets at night by special duty men. It was decided that P. C. Hodgkiss be promoted to the rank of sergeant. The MAYOR in moving the confirmation of the minutes explained that the appointment of the addi- tional constables was rendered necessary as the com- mittee had had to place five Men on special duty on account of the opening of the tram system. Alderman Ht7TCHINsoN seconded.

Councillor TINNION said he was pleased to see what was proposed with regard to the watching of the markets. He had had many complaints from the market tenents of the loss they had sustained by theft from time to time, because of the want of police supervision. He hoped the committee would see their way to accept the suggestion of the Watch Committee for the proper watching of the markets and thereby prevent the thefts which were almost of nightly occurrence With regard to the appointment of the four extra men he thought it would be as well to postpone any action until the end of the financial year. He was afraid that unless a number of the committees were, like the Watch Committee, able to show a balance in hand, the rates next year would go up, and it was because of that pro- bability that he recommended the adjournment of the question of increasing the police force. Alderman FAIRCLOUGH painted out that the four extra men would cost annually £303, half of which would come from the Government exchequer. Councillor PEMBERTON agreed with Councillor' Tinnion that' the question should be deferred on the ground of expense. The MAYOR pointed out that the Chief Constable had made out a report showing that the work of the police force was greatly increased by the passing of the recent Acts of Parliament. The Chief Constable further pointed I out that if the force was made to accord with the Government standard eleven additional men would be required. Continuing he said there was no question of the Markets Committee agreeing to the proposal of the Watch Committee. He pointed out that more care- ful watching of the markets was made necessary as stallholders now used the markets for warehousing purposes though originally they did not do so. Councillor TINNION : The tenants pay an additional market toll.

The MAYOR; There was Gd. put on to allow the tenants to have lock-up stalls. Councillor A. PEACOCK proposed as an amendment that the matter be deferred to the end of the year. The MAYOR: The man in charge tells you he cannot carry on without additional policemen. (A voice: "Bosh.") . _
Councillor A. PEACOCK expressed the opinion that the town was well looked after.

Councillor SKELLAND seconded the amendment. Alderman SMETHURST said the matter had been care- fully thrashed out by the committee. It was not what the Chief Constable wanted, but what the Government Inspector wanted. Alderman HUTCHINSON said the question of increasing the police force could not be deferred any longer. It should be borne in mind that since the force was last increased the tramways had been introduced, and four or live constables were required to watch the lines. Councillor Loan: Have we had any communication from the Home Office? The MAYOR: The resolution is in accordance with a recommendation made by the Government Inspector. Alderman Surros : What will be the cost of the four police during the present financial year? The DEPUTY-MAYOR: £5O. Half of which will be refunded by the Government. Alderman Surros : That is not worth thinking about.
The amendment was lost by a big majority nod the minutes carried in their entirety. IMPROVED HEALTH.

Alderman SIITTOII, in moving the adoption of the Health Committee's minutes, observed that the health of the town appeared to be steadily improving. The scarlet fever epidemic had subsided and there was now no smallpox. (Hear, hear.) •

div.head: REDUCTION IN THE PRICE OF MANURE.
div.p: REDUCTION IN THE PRICE OF MANURE.
The Council on the recommendation of the Sanitary Works Committee decided to reduce the price of manure manufactured at Longford by ss. per ton. DRAINAGE IN THE ORFORD DISTRICT. SCHEME APPROVED.

At a meeting of the Paving and Sewerage Committee a scheme prepared by the Borough Surveyor for the drainage of the Orford District was considered and ap- provedb. In his report upon the scheme' the Borough Surveyor pointed out that the system of gravitating the sewage could not be adopted on account of the level of the district. He suggested that the sewage should be conveyed in pipes to the corner of Orford Avenue and there raised by means of duplicate Shone ejectors and emptied into the existing sewer. The ejectors worked per- fectly automatically and cost annually for keepiir, in repair only one per cent of the original cost. keeping total cost of the scheme would be £2,000. New sewers would have to be put down in Gorsey Lane and Alder Lane. _ _ _

Councillor TINNION in moving the adoption of the minutes dwelt in detail upon the scheme. He pointed out that the ejectors would be worked by means of compressed air from the plant already at work at the Longford gas works. Altogether he thought the scheme was the most efficient and economical the Council could adopt. (Elear, hear.) The repayment of the £2,000 which they would have to borrow would be extended over a period of 30 years. Alderman EVANS said he was sorry it was proposed to empty the sewage into _the already overworked sewer in Fennel-street. The Fennel-street sewer was at the present time flooded by an even normal sewer and he was afraid it would not be capable of doing the extra work which it was proposed should be put upon it. Councillor TINNION said that in his opinion the sewer would be able to take the extra sewage. When .the time came he would be quite prepared to go in for a thorough and extensive scheme, but he was not prepared to ask the borough to spend £lOO,OOO at the present time. The committee had dealt with sewers as they found them, and he believed it was right to say that in extraordinary showers—those storms they spoke about as being the worse for years—the Fennel-street sewer was too small. Really, they had no other means of dealing with the sewage, but at very considerable cost it could be run into a sewer at Winwick-road and continued past the Gas Works and into Sankey Brook. But he thought they had putquite enough" rain water" into Sankey Brook—(hear, hear and laughter)—and he was not in favour of putting any more into it. He thought the committee had done the bet thing possible under the circumstances. The scheme was approved.

div.head: NEW DEPARTURE.
div.p: A NEW DEPARTURE.

At a meeting of the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee, held on the 21st November, it was resolved: ‘: That the- Chairman Deputy-Chairman, Alderman Hutchinson and Councillor Pemberton be appointed a sub-committee to inspect and report from time to time upon the delivery and quality of paving materials pur- chased by the committee." The minutes were approved,

div.head: QUALITY OF GAS.
div.p: THE QUALITY OF GAS.

When the minutes of the Gas Committee were under consideration, Councillor PEMBERTON said he had received several complaints with regard to the quality of the gas. The gentleman who complained he said, had only been three years in Warrington and might be excused. He came from Sheffield where the gas cost 1.10 and was about twice the illuminating power of Warrington gas. Councillor TrNsroN : Nonsense. Councillor PEMBERTON : That is what I said. Counciilor MINION : Impossible. Councillor PEMBERTON : Of course, it's quite impos- sible. That is only what he says; not what I say. (Laughter). Continuing, he said he thought the gas consumers were deserving of consideration, and should not be penalized to make big profits. They were larger contributors to the rates than those who did not use much gas. The minutes were carried. COMPENSATION FOR A TRAM CONDUCTOR. COUNCILLOR WILKINSON AND .THE NON-TRADERS.

At a meeting-of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee the Town Clerk reported that the action hart been commenced at the suit of Joseph C. Knox for damages under the Workmen's Compensation Act, and that acting on medical advice he had settled the same. by the payment of £5O and costs. Alderman SMETHURST moved and Councillor Wrracm- SON seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor LORD said he understood that the corn - mittee were threatened with an action by Knox about nine months ago, but they were advised that he had no case. Now the Council were asked to sanction the pay- ment of compensation. Councillvr PEMBERTON contended that Knox had been hounded from his situation because he was a work- ingman. He hoped the result of the case would be a warning to those members of the committee who in his (Councillor Pemberton's) opinion did not give the man fair play. Councillor WILKINSON described Councillors Pember- ton and Lord as gallery players "and contended that their object in pressing the matter was to "keep up the character of the Non-Trading fraternity." The com- mittee were quite willing to compensate Knox on learning the full circumstances. They were originally told that there was no working machinery in the build- ing where the accident happened, but as it had now been proved that there was working machinery, the money had been awarded. He advised Councillors Lord and Pemberton to investigate these matters in com- mittee and not bring them before the Council. Councillor S'TOTT thought the case ought to be an object lesson to the committee as to the taking of advice.

• Councillor TINNION thought the case had been exceed. ingly unfairly put by Councilln,s Lord and Pemberton. It was evidently the intentl,,,l to lead the public to the opinion that Knox had been deliberately harshly treated by the committee. He would be very pleased if a committee could be appointed to investigate the whole of the circumstances of the case. He believed the committee would come out of the inquiry very well indeed. The case had been unsatisfactory from the beginning. (Hear, hear). It was kept alive by several members of the committee, he supposed for the sake of cheap popularity. The committee did what they thought was the best in awarding Knox £5O. He had had what was called a "soft job" for nine months and had been paid his wages. It was only when the manager said he could not afford for:the discipline of the tramways to have men doing "soft jobs" and that the best thing the committee could do would be to get rid of him by paying a certain sum, that the case was settled. The Town Clerk on the instructions of the committee took medical advice and informed them that it was desirable to settle the case for £5O. A doctor's bill of something like .£l7 was paid by the committee, and they thought they had acted fairly and honestly towards Knox.

Alderman SmETHuasT also contended that Knox had been very fairly treated, in fact his opinion was that the man had been paid more than he deserved. He was offered work in the car-shect, but did not take advantage of it. The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: SMOKE-NUISANCE.
div.p: THE SMOKE-NUISANCE.
Interesting Lecture by Dr. Markel.

A very interesting lecture was given by Dr. Marke/ at last week's meeting of the Polyglot Society, on "Smoke and Soot." A large number of the members attended the meeting. and formed a most appreciative audience.

The LECTURER, after some preliminary remarks with regard to Gorabustion generally, and explaining the laws relating to it, gave in some detail the conditions neces- sary for the burning of all fuel without smoke. He pointed out that the bituminous fuel in this neighbour- hood and generally in the north of England present% some difficulty in that respect, but by no means such as could not be overcome by the practi- cal application of those simple laws of Chemistry which govern the combustion of such fuel. He said that black smoke pouring out from a chimney was invariably a sign either of Ignorance on the part of the works' manager or a token of the exercise of false economy—the first a state of affairs which could only be overcome in time by education, and the latter by the insistance of the governing bodies who should force manufacturers to realise that the health and welfare of the general public must be considered by them, and that they must adopt those processes which modem scientific research has shown will not only remove the nuisance complained of, but will in almost all cases produce better economical results at the same time. The Lecturer pointed out, and proved in figures, that the neglect of manufacturers to make use of the laws of combustion led to enormous losses,, of which the visible loss in fuel, as shown in the clouds of smoke issuing from the chimney stacks, is but a very small part. The loss through smoke alone may in the worst case amount to 3 percent. of the fuel burnt. The loss of fuel in unconsumed gases always accompanying smoke is far and away greater than that presented by the soot itself, and is moreover much more important inasmuch as these gases are exceedingly poisonous. Some interesting figures were given with regard to he quantities of soot in Manchester. The amount collected in a certain area, three miles from the centre- of Manchester, amounted to over three tons per square mile in 10 days, and nearly ten tons in the centre of the city. The amount was actually collected in ten days on snow. The enormous loss to property, harm to vegeta- tion and animal life, which accompanies the presence of smoke and the poisonous gases always accompanying it were gone into. Also the part domestic fire-places play in the formation of fogs and the remedies, especially for manufacturers to avoid the formation of smoke were dealt with.

A London fog was illustrated by experiment, and a collection of substances were shown Iwhich were pro- duced from Manchester soot. Especially • interesting_ was the flint shewn that this soot contained a dye, and samples of cobton dyed light and dark brown were shown.

In the discussion which ensued the wish was expressed that this important subject should have been ventilated before a larger audience. It was pointed out that we in this town were very great sufferers from this evil, Ind it was urged that an action which could tend to influence public opinion and cause action on the part of the Corporation should be looked upon in the light of the public duty. Mr. May expressed a wish that the valuable information contained in the lecture $ hould be brought before the notice of a wider public, and pointed out that this could only be effectually done with the aid of the Press.

div.head: &?A5--
div.p: W3IIEN'S CHAT.

The Coming of Christmas.—The anticipations of hristmas are fully reflected in the extra bustle and rightness of the shops, and the Queen, and Princess of Wales have both been busy this week,making selections of toys andsuitablegifts for Christmas presents. This is no light task for members of the Royal Family, as though unlike the majority of less exalted personages, they, have not to consider the limitations of the purse, yet it is not an easy matter to select gifts for others who already have everything one can think of. Yet the Queen invariably manages to overcome- this difficulty and her gifts are selected with a care and judgment that makes them more than doubly prized by their recipients Thenithe poor and old folk amongst the cottagers round Windsor and Sandringham come in for a large share of her Majesty's attention as, in addition to the usual distribution of coals and food, the Queen often gives a warm garment or other comfort where it is specially needed. Not as in the Fairy Tales.—Childhood always pictures Princesses scattering handfuls of gold wherever they go, but the little folks belonging to the Royal Family are of course never permitted to entertain loose ideas about money,' It is a great delight to the Royal children to be able to go to the shops and buy what they like, but when this happens it is the modest half-crown they are given to spend, and not the handfuls of gold which the fairy-tales bestow upon them. Moreover they are just as keen as other children to lay out their money to the best advantage, and they often succeed in obtaining wonderful value for it, though all the time it is pre- tended by the shopkeeper andhis assistants not to know who they are. " Toyland."—The general preference among the leisured classes for toys of home manufacture 'is, happily, very noticeable this Christmas. "Made in Britain," or" made in Ireland "may be read on vast numbers of the labels, and toys so marked are going off more quickly than those of foreign origin. From the Sister Isle we have this year the most delightful dolls, dressed in Irish peasant costume, also giant animals fashioned from gaily colored cloth, her Majesty and thelPrincess of Wales having purchased these particular wares generously. Most of the beautiful little models of smart carriages, which may cost anything from one 'pound to five, are of British make, but curiously enough the horses between the &shafts are• usually of foreign origin. Of course the motor car is well to the fore, from the painted tin varieties sold for a few pence to the highly finished racing cars, with "hooter," the willow basket that fits Pon behind, extra tyres, spare parts, and masked chauffeurs. The war too is responsible for many new and jfascinating toys, and altogether the little folks are catered for, as surely they have never been before. An Old-World Gift.—Among lovers, a very favourite gift this Christmas is a painting of the eyes, in minia- ture, after the manner of Richard Cosway. This minia- ture can be set in a ring, or used to adorn a watch or cigarette case, the air of mystery and secrecy surround- ing the keepsake, greatly adding to its charm. Dress for the rheatre.—Those women who happen to have by them short lengths of old brocade, fancy silk, or velvet, in delicate shades of pastel colouring, should set about the building of the little theatre coat- patterns of which may be found in all the fashion papers—and which is taking the place of the all too- popular theatre blouse. These dainty coats are cut square at the throat, and their sole triKaming consists of a generous supply of real lace ruffles, and some really handsome buttons. They are donned with white skirts which may be of silk, or any of the thin wool stuffs. Silks of Home Manufacture.—The majority of the soft ivory white satins, in such favour among brides, and for evening gowns, are of English manufacture, modistes having discovered that none other drapes so well, or hangs so artistically. In point of durability too, we seem to have at length discovered that these lovely home manufactured satins can more than hold their own against those varieties which flood the market from abroad. Next in favour for evening gowns is chiffon velvet, and rich taffetas glace silk—" mousseline finished "—the prevailing tint being ivory white, or a delicate tone of a rose-leaf pink, which latter appears to be in perfect harmolty with the present revival of Louis XVI. modes. The•cmze for entire gowns of dyed laces —brown Valenciennes over amber chiffon being first favourite—still exists, but it is one that will possess ra great fascination for the masies, and will therefore, be quickly given up by exclusive dressers. Concerning Coiffures,—The huge plait wound flatly round and ending in a few curls or coils on the top of the head, is a novel form of hairdressing,and one that is finding great favour anioug those to whom Nature has been lavish in the matter of a wealth of tresses. The plait shews above the pompadour, but all suggestion of harshness is impossible, for the hair is softly puffed out beside it, and by this means the hard line of the "braid" is broken. Generally speaking, the mode is a most becoming one, and suitable with both day and evening toilettes. Riding Astride.—Women are occasionally seen riding astride in the country and in the hunting field, but it is anything but a graceful spectacle and those people who think the custom will become the fashion, are quite mistaken. Several reasons are given in favour of the change, the most important being the view that it is safer. But this is not so, and few women riders of experience would give up the crutch of the side-saddle

Cairo-street Literary and Debating Society. At a meeting of the above Society on Tuesday evening, the members discussed the conduct of Warren Hastings as govenor-general of Bengal. There was a large attendance of both ladies and gentlemen, and an interesting and instructive evening was spent. The i scussion was opened by the Rev. C. Harvey Cook, who moved the impeachmedt of Warren Hastings. i Mr. J. S. Hill opposed him, and spoke effectively n defence of the governor-general. Several members expressed their opinions in regard to the conduCt of Hastings, and there was a marked tendency on the part of the speakers to regard his methods of administration with leniency. Of those who took part in the voting, four supported the impeachment while eleven expressed themselves in favour of the defence.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, December 10, 1904. FASHIONS OF TO-DAY. EVENTS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 10, 1904. FASHIONS OF TO-DAY. EVENTS OF THE WEEK.

Furs are now a necessity, for at this season of the year the cold out of doors-necessitates warm wraps, and these are provided this year at prices to sait all purses. There are smart little coatees of plush or wbollen materials made -to -,-losely imitate various -furs which are cut on the lines of the really good expensive models and are trimmed with appliques of silk braid, white kid bordered with passementerie, or silk or velvet, some- times used separately and alone, and at others intermingled into a tasteful collar of the flat or rolled type. These dainty coats are sold at a very reasonable price and are generally lined with a flowered silk or satin. To prove a really serviceable winter wrap, however, an interlining of wadding or flannel is necessary as the imitation fur is, of course, not nearly so va rm as the real article. It

atld three great tiers of seats sweep rouna the house. The stage is the largest in London, being eight feet bigger than Covent Garden, and seventeen feet bigger than Drury Lane. It is fifty-five feet wide from the auditorium and seventy feet high. The scenery will be shifled by machinery and runs on great roller; forty yards long. The stage consists of three revolving platforms capable of a speed of twenty ;Idles either separately or all together, and one of •the first representations to be given is to be a realistic Derby, for which twenty thorough- breds have been trained. There will also be chariot races and all sorts of shows hitherto impossible on the London stage. Another of the great spectacular shows pro- mised for the opening is a ‘battle between Russians and Japanese. •

div.head: PRETTY SKIRT.
div.p: PRETTY SKIRT.

would quite pay the purchaser of a coat of th. kind for the trouble and time occupied to carefully unpick the lining of silk or satin and cut from it a lining of wadding or one made from a double piece of ordinary red flannel, which should be stitched together, as other- wise it will not keep in its place and might in this way spoil the fit of the coat. The arm- holes of the coat may require to be a little eased before replacing the silk lining, as the interlining will, of course, make the coat fit tighter. To the girl of limited means these pietty little coats come as a godsend as they are so inexpensive when iewed in comparison with the real article, and yet they look, if anything, smarter and better fitting, and if warmly lined make a delightful (pit of doors wrap. They , are especially convenient be- cause they can be worn with any sort of skirt and in this way one can greatly. vary street dress, and a cloth walt:ing costume can be worn with its own coat as with one of the kind described. •

A more lengthy and more dressy skirt is `a necessity on many occasions when the short walking skirt would- seem out of place, and my first sketch depicts a smart black cash- mere skirt of this kind made with numerous tiny tucks and terminating in a furl. flounce headed and edged by a ruching of black taffeta silk. A skirt of this style would look exceedingly smart with a black coat of

imitation caracule trimmed with a fiat applique of taffeta silk and passementerie round the collarless neck and down the front. The lining of the skirt should be of rustling silk for preference, but as this is a luxury which cannot be afforded by all, as it is apt to cut at the ,edges and therefore does not wear very long, 1 should suggest one or other of the new lining materials which, if they do not give out the charming froufrou sound so dear to the feminine heart, are soft and pretty besides durable. Aloireen is a very service- able lining, but is rather too stiff to line a soft clinging material such as cashmere. -Many smart wanen are wearing glace silk skirts, but as these are sold as cheaply as a couple of guineas I cannot conscientiously recommend them, as a cheap silk is never satisfactory for it soon wears wherever there is the slightest friction, and the price of the really good silk skirts puts them beyond the means of most people, and thereore a cloth skirt of one kind or the other will be found a much better in- vestment than a cheap silk. The charming hat in my second illustration is of the low, broad, flat-crowned style so much in vogue and so very becoming to most people. The hat, in this instance, is of white felt trimmed with a broad band of pink velvet ribbon arranged in loops at either side, while a dark red rose of the cabbage order rests on the hair under one side of the brim. The hat is of the picturesque order and its becoming- ness is further enhanced by the shower of rosebuds which depends from the curved brim

div.head: MODERN BLOUSE
div.p: A MODERN BLOUSE

which is depressed at the back, and form [a sort of cache-peigne of pink and green. For restaurant or theatre wear the style is a charming one as the low flat crown would not interfere with the cojnfort of anyone sitting behind: as is the case with the Gainsborough or any other picture hats. There is nothing on which the success of a woman's toilette depends more than her hat, and however pretty a face or smart a gown the effect and charm will be lost if an unbecoming or un- suitable chapeau forms the crowning feature. The veil which accompanies it also pl4s an important part in the tout ensemble, and the well dressed woman varies her veils, as what proves becoming one day may not be so the following. A clear ground with or without a small chenille spot is best. Blouses are still much in evidence, and a pretty blouse such as forms the subject of my last sketch would be a welcome Christmas gift to most girls, whether at home or abroad. I think in selecting a 'blouse for a gift for someone else it is wisest not to choose a coloured one as it might not be a shade that was becoming to the recipient, or it might not harmonise with the' other contents of her wardrobe. Therefore, in selecting a soft white or ivory silk blouse trimmed with some prettily patterned lace or insertion one cannot fail to please. Soft oriental satin blouses are also very charming and look well worn underneath a coat which opens in front to show the pretty blouse beneath. These are generally trim. med with a heavier ma.ke of lace than the lighter silk blouses and are, therefore, per- haps handsomer looking.

div.head: ITALIAN CHRISTENING.
div.p: THE ITALIAN CHRISTENING.

The Prince of Piedmont made his debut into public .life last Sunday when he was baptised, and the great event was surrounded by every possible sign of outside pomp. This was not only with the idea of impress- ing the populace and adding to the popu- larity and stability of the throne, but to atone for the lack of pomp on the religious side of the ceremony. Owing to the quarrel between the Quirinal and the Vatican, the Pope ,refused to accede to the request of the King to send a high official of the church or to al!aw one of the Cardinals to perform

_.:UR OF CONNAUGHT. the ceremony, though he qualified this by sending his blessing to the little prince privately. This was a great disappointment to King Victor Emmanuel, who had wished to make the occasion an opportunity for reconciliation, but Queen Elena is more in- different to the claims of the Roman Catholic Church and treated the matter lightly. So, to compensate for the religious side of the cere- mony, King Victor Emmanuel organised a great gathering of laity. There were repre- sentatives from all the foreign courts with their suites, all the Italian princes with suites, the Diplomatic Corps, the Premier and all the Parliamentary and public officials, the chief naval and military authorities, and the: Wearers of the collar of the An- unziata, who rank as cousins of the King. Prince Arthur of Connaught, attended by Lord Grenfell, represented King Edward, who stood as one of the Prince of Piedmont's sponsors. He arrived on Saturday morning, together with the Duke of Oporto, who represents the King of Portugal, and they were met at the station by the King and the Count of Turin, together with the repre- sentatives of the two Embassies. Prince Arthur is the guest of the King of Italy at the Quirinal and was most warmly welcomed on every side. The christening ceremony went off without a hitch, and the little prince was named Umberto after his assassinated grand- Jather. . ."

div.head: NORTH SEA INQUIRY.
div.p: THE NORTH SEA INQUIRY.

The North Sea Inquiry seems somewhat to be hanging fire, and things are by no means progressing as fast as was expected. The latest news is that Admiral Dewey has re- fused to serve on the Inquiry and that President Roosevelt has filled up the Ameri- can vacancy by the appoint-
ment -of Rear- Admiral Charle H. Davis, whr

"Dixie," from ADMIRAL CHARLES H. DAVIS. which he was -- _ _

Admiral Davis has been connected with the various expeditions for the determination of the difference of longi- tude by means of submarine cables and is considered one of the cleverest officers under the Stars and Stripes. Admiral Kazrakoff, Russia's representative, has been sitting in the Supreme Prize Court at St. Petersburg, hearing appeals from Vladivostock. In both the cases of the Thea and the Arabia he annulled the sentence of -confiscation, but upheld the Russian right of seizing and ovek hauling suspicious vessels. The latest de- tachment of the Baltic Fleet is now safely out of British waters, but there is a rumour that the five battleships with cruisers and torpedoes left to guard the shores of Russia will he sent to the Far East at once, so as to make Russia as strong, if not stronger, than Togo. None of the ships left, however, are of much consequence, and the capture of 203-Metre Hill will release practically the whole of Togo's fleet, as every vessel in Port Arthur Harbour will now be reduced to matchwood.

div.head: COLISEUM.
div.p: THE COLISEUM.

Of the making of places of amusement in London there would seem to be no end, and the latest is the great Coliseum, in St. Martin's Lane, which is to be opened on Monday week as the first of the Christmas attractions. It has taken nearly a year to build at the cost of Lioo,ooo, under the

LONDON'S NEW PLACE OF AMLISEMEN, direct supervision of Mr. Oswald Stoll, who is to manage it. The idea is to provide amusement, rest and recreation for the public at all times of the day: To begin with, there will be four performances daily, namely, at noon, at three, at six, and at nine, and these will embrace two totally different shows. In , addition, there are to be lounges, reading-rooms, winter gardens, and restaurants in the building, and bands will play between the shows for the amusement of those who are waiting. Another of Mr. Stoll's new ideas is to have a permanent trained chorus of fifty voices in two alcoves off the stage so the,: each " turn " shall have .proper support in the chorus. The decoration is marble and gold, magnificent in its size and solidity*

div.head: NEW GOVERNOR-GENERAL- OF CANADA.
div.p: THE NEW GOVERNOR-GENERAL- OF CANADA.

At the end of laQt week Earl Grey left this country to take up his pdst of Governor- General of Canada and was seen off by a select crowd of enthusiastic friends. Though many regret his departure from his sphere of usefulness in this country, it is generally felt that he is essentially the man for the post of Governor - General of Canada. Not only has he proved his ability all through his career but his name is widely known through- out the Empire as an Imperialist. Moreover, though a peer, he is not hide bound by con- ventions, but inclines to bedemocr a tic, which will go down well with the Canadians. Strangely enough, the only point of complaint against, him when Administrator of Rhodesia from 1896-7 was that he was inclined to be too democratic, but in Canada that • will not be accounted a fault. In England he is little known in the "smart set," as the life of London does not appeal either to Lady Grey or) himself, and he prefers to be at home on his Northumbrian estates. There he tried to introduce a system of co-operation between landlord and tenants, but it did not meet with striking success. His hobby, however, is agriculture, and he is full of enthnsiasms.

REY. He is a tall, dark, slight man of fifty-tnrec with an alert, intelligent face, and he is quick both in thought and action. His knowledge of agriculture will go down well in Canada and will prove a bond of sympathy between the Canadians and himself. In 1877 he married Miss Holford, who shares his work with him and will be of the greatest assistance to him as Governor-General. They have a son and heir, Viscount Howick, who is just five and twenty years of age.

div.head: DAWN OF LIBERTY IN RUSSIA.
div.p: THE DAWN OF LIBERTY IN RUSSIA.

It is hoped that at last the dawn of liberty has set in in Russia, and that before long steps will definitely be taken to estab- lish a more or less popular constitution. When Prince Sviatopolk-Mirski consented tc succeed M. de Plehve in the thankless post of. Minister of the Interior it was only upon the
distinct under-
standing that he
should -have a free • hand to
bring about re-
forms. The Tsar :onsented, but
the Prince has met with the most bitter
ppposition from I. Pobi e d- no steff and Aber persons tnfluentialat Court. How-

ever, nearly a month ago he , presented a list !of forty-three articles em- bodying various reforms, which he proposed to pre sent to the congress of the Zemstyos or provincial councils. He met with a rebuff from the Tsar, and in consequence tendered his resignation, whereupon the Tsar gave a grudging consent. The Congress of the Zemstvos was allowed to meet on the island of Vassili-Ostroff, but the papers were forbidden to report or publish any news of the meeting. It was attended by seventy- five members, and the question of the Constitution was discussed. The principal proposal made was to pension off the members of the Council of State and to replace them by two representatives from each province, popularly elected. Other proposals were the freedom of the Press and religious thought, equality of land rights for all classes of the population, that the people have a vote in the legislation of the country and popular representation, and the immovability of judges, as in England, to assure impartial administration of justice. At first it was announced that the Tsar had refused to entertain the suggestions, and then it was rumoured that he was ready to grant the ten proposals submitted to him, except the one dealing with the popular control of the Budgets.

The case was removed to Belfast as in the previous trials there had been rumours of intimidation, and the judge appealed to the jury, who were unwilling 10 serve, to do their duty without fear. The case dates back to April r6th of last ycar, when the victim, a young farmer named Flana,an, left his home in Co. IVl•naghan for Clones Market with a con- s,i(ler:ll,le sum of money in his -possession and ~iisapp..ared without leaving a trace • behind Lim. He had been seen in Fee's company the • day of his disappearance, and eight months lat cr, when manure was being carted from Fee's yard at the back of • his house, a body, half burnt away by quicklime, was fcunc:: in the pit. It was identified as Flanagan's, and there could be no doubt that he had been murdered, as his throat was cut from ear to ear. Beside him was found a butcher's knife wilik pig's bristles adhering to it, and Fee was by trade a butcher. He was arrested last January and protested his innocence, relying upon an alibi. He was most ably defended at all three trials, but at the last the evidence brought forwa-fd by Mr. O'Shaughnessy for the Croim proved too strong, and after a long deliberation the jury found him guilty

div.head: I.WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT
div.p: I.WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT
COUNCIL.

The Closing of Kiln-lane Footpath. The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on iWednes- day. Mr. Halton presided, and there were also present: —Dr. Murray, Messrs. ForshavP, Thompson, Mather, Knowles, and Backhouse, together with Messrs. J. C. Sutton kclerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), F. W. Ker- foot (inspector), B. S. Newlombe (surveyor), H. H. Burnage (assistant surveyor), and Dr. Sephton (medical officer). REPRESENTATION ON HE PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY. Mr.Surros read a letter from the Town Clerk stating that Alderman Sutton's term of officeas the representa- tive of the Corporation and the District Council, on the Port Sanitary Authority, had now expired, ' ind asking for nominations for the appointment. He (the Clerk) had replied sayingthe Council would agree to Alderman Sutton's re-election.

It was decided to recommend Alderman Sutton's re-election. PADGATE SEWERA.GE SCHEME. The CLERK reported that he had received an inquiry from the Local Government Board with regard to the Padgate Sewerage Scheme. That was the third inquiry he had received and to the previous ones he had replied stating that the matter was still under consideration. He thought that day the Council should reply at greater Length. Mr. NEWCOMBE said the Corporation were undertak- ing certain Work for treatment of sewage from the Orford Ward,upon which he had drawn up a report which he thought would be worth while considering. Mr. Newcombe then read his raport in which he suggested that thePadgate, Orford, Longford and Winwick sewage should be emptied into the Corporation sewer in Orford- lane and passed- through the Shone ejectors which the Corporation had decided to put down. The total cost Of the work proposed by the Corporation was £2,000 with an annual cost of £5O. If the inclusion of District Council sewage doubled the necessary capacity it would mean a cost, in the first instance of £l,OOO and anannual cost of £5O. That would form a special charge upon the districts named.

Mr. MATHER thought the matter should be thoroughly investigated and the question of cost gone into before any definite steps were taken. The SURVEYOR was instructed to confer with the Borough Surveyor and report to the Medical Officer, so that he could incorporate any proposed scheme in his annual report to the Local Government Board.
THE CLOSING OF KILN-LANE FOOTPATH.
DISTRICT COUNCIL REQUESTED TO TAKE ACTION.

_ . The CLERK read a letter from the Clerk to the Burton- wood Parish Council stating he had been instructed to ask the District Council to take whatever steps were necessary to secure the use of Kiln-lane footpath to the inhabitants of Burtonwood, it being well attested to be an ancient right of the parish. Mr. Sutton pointed out that the matter wis under discussion at the last meet- ing of the District Council and was adjourned. Mr. FoßsHew moved that the Surveyor be instructed to remove the obstruction which had beenplaced across the footpath. He thought the Council had been wrongly advised in the matter. That was the first step which should have been taken.

Mr. S UTTON : If these people complain they have been deprived of a right they should remove the obstacle. If their doing so leads to trouble this Coun- cil would probably take the matter up. Continuing he said the position Mr. Forshaw desired them to take up might involve the Council in some very serious and expensive, litigation over a footpath about which they knew nothing. In Frodsham a man named Edwards re- moved an obstruction which had been placed across a footpath and was involved in litigation which only ended in an appeal to the House of Lords. He thought someone should remove the obstruation and then if there were future difficulties it would be reasonable for the Council to consider whether they should take action or not., Mr. Forshaw had originally removec: the ob- struction and no harm had been done except for the small harm that Mr. Forshaw had been summoned.

Mr. FORSHAW : If you had left me alone I would have left the fence alone. I took the fence down and it cost me £2O, and I was told by our leading member that I had been guilty of an act of lawlessness. Con- tinuing Mr4Forshaw contended it was now, according to the duty of the Council to take the matter up, and submitted that the dignity and honour of the Council were involved in the question. It they were going to let that matter pass,people would close other footpaths just as they liked. If they did let the matter drop the people of Buttonwood would petition the County Council. Mr. Forshaw contended that if it came to a matter of law the Council should be prepared to fight. Mr. KNOWLES : The Bible advises us to learn th e strength of our opponents before going to war. Mr. FORSHAW : Perhaps the Bible is your private property. (Laughter.) Mr. gIITTON : Mr. Forshaw is now advising the Council to do something. He complains about my advising the Parish Council to do it. Mr. FORSHAW : You did notadvise the Parish Cou- ncil. You advised me.

Mr. SurroN : I did not advise you personally. I advised the Parish Council. Mr. 11,u;roN asked for a seconder to Mr. Forshaw's motion, bu,t none was forthcoming. Mr.HALTON: Then Mr. Forshaw falls to the ground. (Laughter).

div.head: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

Dr. SEPHTON reported that during the month there had beenl6 births and 33 deaths. The death-rate was equal to 33 per 1,000, as against 34 the average of the past three months, and 37-8 for the corresponding period of last year. Twenty-two of the deaths occurred at the County Asylum, exclusive of which the death-rate for the district was equal to 11-5 per thousand. There had been an outbreak of scarlet fever at Winwiok, and he had thought it advisable that the schools in that dis- trict should be closed fot three weeks.

SANKEY BROOK. The INSPECTOR reported that he had served a notice upon Messrs. Joseph Crosfleld and Sons calling upon them to remove an obstruction in Sankey Brook caused by their tip. He had received a letter in reply point- ing out that their tenancy of the tip expired in June.
COUNTY PAYMENTS. 110 fr. NEWCOMBE reported that he had received £1,431 from the County Council on account of work done on the county roads. There was still outstanding the sum of £2,182 13s. 3d.

div.head: . MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: . MOTOR NOTES.

In the columns of the" Automobile Club Journal" we notioe that one of the observers engaged in the recent tri-car trials has some criticism to offer concern- ing the judges' reports on the results obtained. - The Auto-Cycle Club was the subject of considerable merriment atthe recent Stanley Show. It appears that the elaborate certificates awarded in regard to the worthy performance of motor-cycles during the Thousand Miles Trials are decorated with a device (which has surely done service before under more appro- priate circumstances !) representing a procession of motor cars—and with not a single motor-cycle to be seen! A ludicrous mistake has also been made in the engraving of the medals awarded inconnection with the same event. Instead of representing that these are pre- sented to the different riders who came through with flying colours, the name of the makers of the various machines have been engraved. It is really surprising that such egregious errors can be made, and, having been made, can be finally passed. An effort is being made to boom the tri-car ; but not- withstanding its recent successes at Islington where samples of this type of machine were to be seen in great numbers,vve very much doubt whether it will really hold its own for very long. If it could only be pro- duced at about two-thirds its present price there is admittedly &certain class to whom it would appeal;but it does not seem that, from a commercial standpoint, this can be done. The result) is that a well-designed tri-car, having water-cooling and a multi-speed gear, costs very little under one hundred bounds, and this is a serious sum to ask from the average champion of this type of machine. The prices of the cars themselves will undoubtedly be reduced before long, and when thiatiappy consumma- tion arrives the tri-car will certainly have far less chance of popularity than it now enjoys. The reduc- tion in car prices has been commenced by Messrs. Humber, who have placed a four-cylinder light car on the market at two hundred and fifteen guineas, and, con- sidering that this is a well-designed and comfortably arranged three seated vehicle, fitted with all modern improvements, it is easy to see that the present prize of an ordinary two-seated, single-cylinder voiturette must be reduced. Even now one can buy a very nice little voiturette at about £125, or just about five-and- twenty pounds more than is asked for some tri-cars. It is rather a problem how to dress suitably and yet tastefully for motoring. The regular long-distance tourists generally have a most terrifying appearance, particularly in the winter, when their fur coats, warm caps, and ghoulish-looking goggles are most conspicu- ous. The last-named accessories, of course, is always necessary whatever the weather, if fast driving s to be indulged in, and great care needs to be taken in choos- ing a suitable pattern. In many of the cheaper kinds they are just finished off with a fringing of chenille and this does not protect the eye at all, but rather induces a worse draught—and, consequently, ' a great risk of inflammation—than if none at all were worn. Those should always be selected which are provided with a good-sized continuation piece, preferably of chamois leather. With flaps of this kind coming well down on the chef bones.. there is no chance of draught being felt by he eyes. 1 ""4
