div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
DECBSIBER 10th. 1904.

There is a subsi- THE PLIGHT OF PORT dence in the Russian ARTHUR. Press agitation for the passage of the Dardanelles ny the Black Sia squadron. Official circles at St. Petersburg seem to think the point is not so simple as it appears to the Russian Admiral who is to serve on the Internationsl Com- mission. He is for sending the squadron through the Straits, and bidding Great Britain go hang. Less impetuous judges in Russia are not so sure that Great Britain will be disposed of so easily. Besides, they have the misgiving that if the Black Sea squadron, which is not remarkably efficient, made a voyage to the Far East without any success, Russia would be dis- tinctly the loser by the breach of the Treaty of Paris. For it is not likely that tue Powers would recognise her right to send a naval force out of the Black Sea, and at the same time 'to forbid the navigation of that sea by foreign warships. When the vital interests of a nation are at stake, necessity is the highest law; but if that law should force the passage of the Dardanelles for the Russian fleet it could scarcely close the Black Sea against all other fleets. This consideration is evidently causing uneasi- ness at S. Petersburg, though the naval authorities there are willing to run any risk of international disturbance for the sake of re- rieving Russia's desperate fortunes in the Far East. It is suspected that the Baltic Fleet is not equal to its mission, and that Russia will be help- less without an overwhelming superiority of naval armament. So the cry is still, "We must send more ships," for without wresting the supremacy of the seas from Japan, Russia cannot hope to loosen the grip of Oyama's armies on Manchuria.

The situation at Port Arthur is uo $v all to the advantage of the besiegers, who are bgginning to reap the reward of sacrifices probably without parallel in military history. They hold a position from which they at e able to pound the Russian ships to pieces, and they have so far broken the strength of the garrison that GENERAL STOESSEL is unable to retake the fort which was supposed to be impregnable. Apparently the Japanese can make it impregnable, though the Russians could not. Within a few hours of the capture of 203-Metre Hill,the besiegers had mounted naval guns which dominated the harbour, and over- mastered the fire from the forts still in the Russian possession. This feat is a most striking illustration of the dauntless energy with which the Japanese have prosecuted this astonishing siege for many months. They must have lost at least 50,000 men, but their spirit is unabated. They can now achieve their main object of crippling the enemy's battleships, even if Stoessel should still cling to his fortifications. It is suggested that when the ships are all sunk the Japanese may regard this work as practically

mshed, and may content themselves with block- ading the remnant of the garrison, after despatch- ing the greater part of General Noca's troops tp reinforce OYAMA. But this is very doubtful. Russia is fighting for her prestige, and if she can keep her flag flying at Port Arthur she will regard that as a tuorAl victory. This is just the victory of which the .1- ipanese wish to deprive her. They mean to overcome the heroic STOESSEL, and make it plain to the world that whatever else may happen, Russi in ne,7er er,Lu. Port Arthur again.

Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P., was treading on dangerous ground on Thursday evening when he alluded to rumours which have been freely circu- lated to the effect that he might not be the candi- date at the next election. A topic of this kind is often best ignored by the person most concerned, for it has an awkward way of gaining a strong hold on the pubiic mind. We are sure Mr. Pierpoint will not like his constituents to discuss his possible absence from the fray, but that is what they are doing, and the fact that he has no intention of resigning will not lessen their curiosity. They will be interested to learn on his own authority that he has not been asked by the Conservative Association to stand. Can the Association have some other iron in the fire? There are Conserva- tives we know who would lie to see Mr. Pierpoint in Cyprus and someone else in Parliament. Mr. A. H. Crosfield is spoken of as a likely 80cc355or— but the topic is tabooed at the Conservative Club. In this uncertain world there are many more improbable events than such a reversal of representation.

Thia Progressive Labour Laague which aims at cementing the alliance between Liberalism and Labour is making excellent progress, and the membership roll is already a large one. The inaugural public meeting in connection with the League will shortly be held. Meanwhile the President, pro teal, of the League (Mr. J. Howes) is actively pursuing his political war, fare in different parts of the country. Recently he has been speaking at Brotton in support of Mr. H. Samuel, and according to the local press he made the speech of the evening. A press cutting states "It is no reflection on Mr. Samuel to, state that the speech of Mr.' Joseph Howes, of Stoke, who enjoys the reputation of;being one of the most effective platform men the party possesses, was the most popular of the evening. A witty address is always welcome to the rniners,but never had they heard such a mirth provoking political attack as they listened to last night." Warrington Liberals can I give further testimony to the oratorical ability of 1 Mr. Howes, and they are hoping to see a good deal of him during the next election fight, when- ever it comes.

There is no questioning the determination of the members of the Property Owners' Association in their opposition to the Workhouse extension scheme, and it is equally evident that their feeling isshared by a large section of the ratepayers. As a representative body of people who would be most directly affected by the projected heavy outlay, the property owners are fully entitled to enter &protest against what they consider an unnecessary expenditure, and their views cannot be lightly set aside. Already the rates of War- rington are burdensome and the prospects of a, relief are very remote—indeed, the increas- clJmands upon the public purse make an addition to the present figure not unlikely. The estimate of £7,000 for the new building will he but an instalment of the actual expenditure, as furnishing, additions to the electrical plant, and other extras will probably double the initial outlay. While recognizing that sooner or later the Guardians will have to face and deal seriously with the pressing accommoda- tion question, we think that in deference to public opinion they might see their way to re-consider this extensive building scheme and look closely around them for additional accommodation in existihg buildings.

The trade depression which is causing such keen distress in some of cur big industrial centres is not, we believe, being felt with anything like the same severity in Warrington. A. is usual about this time of the year operations in the building trade are exceedingly slack, but fortunately although " short time is being worked in various classes of employment, the earnings appear to be sufficient to obviate distress of any magni- tude. The advantage of being a town of many industries" is once more brought home, for it will be recognized that in localities where the vast majority of the population is engaged in one staple manufacture, depression is apt to have much more serious effects. Even in Warrington the conditions are not nearly so cheerful as one would wish, for the Guardians are faced with the difficulty that many able-bodied men who are discharged from the Workhouse to seek employment soon return, hav- ing been unsuccessful in their quest. The Master has submitted a number of practical suggestions for dealing with the problem, and we have no doubt they will receive full and effective con- sideration.

"A light agenda means a long sitting is a new proverb which we offer for the excluiive use of the Warrington Town Council. On Tuesday the printed minntes of the committee proceedings requiring confirmation by the Council cortained few items of importance, but the meeting lasted three hours nevertheless,. and there was much " talkee talkee." Discussions containing many points of interest were raised on such questions as the widening of Warrington Bridge, water works extensions, land purchase for a new school at Latchford, and the enlargement of the police force.

Warrington Bridge widening is not to be further deferred after all. At least that is what a majority of the members of ttie Council have decided after another full-dress debate and vote, but we shall be better satisfied when we see the contractor's men actually on the job. At present the opponents of the seheme seem to have endless opportuaties of blocking progress and agitating for a new bridge. The Council has, on three occa- sions we believe, decided that widening by cantilevers is the only solution to the bridge problem which conforms with present day requirements and the length of the municipal purse. Looking a long way ahead it is, of cours clear that a new bridge will some day be necessary, but the town cannot afford to pay now for what would only be a luxury. The congestion of traffic can be relieved completely by the schema which has already been passed and it should be possible to safeguard users of the upper reaches of the river from any additional complications to naviga- tion. Messrs. Fairclough are the prime movers in the new bridge scheme, and from their point of view such an enterprise on the part of the Cor- poration would be admirable. But, as Alderman Bennett pointed out, "the welfare of Warrington is higher than that of any individual firm, and ought to dominate the action of the Council." We were especially glad to note that, on this occa- sion, Alderman Fairclough took no part in 033 debate. Unless unforseen difficulties arise, we hope that the work of widening will he at once proceeded with.

That there would be trouble in connection with the Water Committee's request for another £20,510 was a foregone conclusion. In the first place the bald statement on the Ininut3s that "the engineer had submitted to the committee a state- ment showing the amount overspent on the water works undertaking under the powers contained in the Act of 1899, and the further sum required to complete the work," coupled with a resolution to apply for sanction to borrow £20,510 was totally insufficient to have any reassuring effect on the minds of the Councillors. It was hoped that thi Chairman of the com- mittee would be able to make such an explanation as would satisfy the members of the Council that the expenditure was necessary, but, unfortunately for the Water Committee, Alderman Francornb's statement was little more explanatory than the resolution on the minutes Substantially it was to the effect that the coin-' mittee was getting three million gallons of water from the new wells, which were only anticipated to provide about a million and a quarter gallonE, with the result that additional capital, to the amount of £20,510 was required to deal with the surplus. Why the fort.inate circumstance that there is such an abundance of water should iovoly3 the commit- tee in so large an expenditure was not made suffiAently clear. To merely say that the money was required "for waterworks purposes " does not suffice and naturally the CouLcil refused to sanction ~.he bOrro wing of the money. Several members demanden that ' the C)m- mittee should take the public more fully into Its confilence, and it seems to us tha3 the committee will have to do so before it will stand

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 10, 1904.

Show of Garments The annual show of garments sent by members of the Warrington Needle.vork Guild, was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday. The display was well attended and will doubtless create an increased interest in the work of this useful organtzation. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Advt. Light Railway Scheme Opposed.

he details of the proposed -‘7Parrington to Knuts- ford light railway scheme have been considered by the Knutsford District Council, and the authority have decided to oppose the proposed Bill. The scheme is exciting keen interest in the Knutsford district.
XMAS PRESENTS.-Try J. S. GARLAND'S, 51 to 55, Bridge-street,Warrington.Splendid selection.—Advt. The Ragged School.

A nun;.-I.7er of girls' jackets (a donation from Messrs. Lord Bros.) have been distributed during the week. The management make a strong appeal for gifts of clothing, books, toys, cakes, sweets, Sr.c., for the poor children's Christmas tree. XMAS PRESENTS.-Try J. S. GARLAND'S, 51 to 55, Bridge-street,Warrineton.Splendid selection.—Advt. Burning Accident.

Lily fessol, aged 4 years, 23, Algernon-street, lies iin the Infirmary n a serious condition suffering from severe burns about the head and arms. She was playing near the fire on Tuesday when her clothing became ignited and slag sustained the injuries described. BEST BOOTS FOR ALL—UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. Found Drowned. The body of Samuel Irons, 227, Kautsford-road, was recovered on Tuesday from the river Mersey near the St. Helens Cable Company's works atßank Quay. At the inquest which was conducted on Wednesday by Mr. Brighouse it was stated that Irons had been missing since the 10th November.—A. verdict of "Found drowned "was returned.

Death of a Local Publican. The death occurred on Sunday night of Mr. Peter White, the well known licensee of the Old Ball Inn, Winwick-ioad. The deceased who was 62 years of age, had been ailing about two years. The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Thursday. Tha Rev. W. Bracecamp performed the last rites. Represent) - tive were present from the Licensed Victuallers' and Wine and Beersellers' Associations.
H. M. ACTITON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63, SANKEY STREET, Warrington.—Advt.
Band of Hope Concert._

A concert organized by the members of the Ebenezer Church Band of Hope Society was held on Monday evening in the above Church, Buttermarket- street.Mr. Thornton presided over a fair attendance.An excellent programme was submitted and the items were highly appreciated. It was commenced with a piano- forte solo, " Blumelied " by Miss Harris. Songs were given by Miss White, an auto-harp selection by Mr. Walmsley, mandoline duets by Miss Lawless and Miss Grace, reading by Mr. Walmsley, and a recitation by Miss E. Baldry. The accompanists were Mr. Monks and Miss Lawless. On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by the Pastor, a vote of thanks was passed to all who had taken part in the proceedings.
H. 3f. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the RI:s7G off TONICS. I 63. SANKEY-STREET. Warrington.—Advt. " Shakespeare " in Warrington.

The coming visit of the famou; F. R. Benson North Shakespearian Co., will be welcomed by all true lovers of dramatic art. To whatever part of the world they might go, our readers would find that people were always ready to acknowledge that one English dramatist had achieved the high water mark of dramatic perfection and it was a source of satisfaction to see with what glorious energy Mr. F. R. Benson was still maintaining the great traditions of he Shakespearian stage. It is to be hoped that the tour of the Colonial Co., he is sending out at Christ- tmas will prove as successful as the North Co., who will visit us next Monday when they will commence a week's engagement at the Court Theatre with " The Taming of the Shrew." Judging by the box plan at Pigot's Music Warehouse, a big week of business is already assured. Mr. Yolland the advance agent will be pleased to arrange with schpols and parties at a reduction.
ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLAS NIENERA.L WATERS.—Advt. A Local Will Dispute.

At the Lancashire Chancery Court on Thursday before Vice-Chancellor Hall, Joseph Smith, Ho_4- lane, Great Sankey, sued his brother and sister, John Smith and Martha Smith, 03, Legh-street, Warrington, for -a declaration that he was entitled in fee simple in possession of two undivided fourth parts of certain lands and hereditaments forming part of the estate of the father of the parties, estate agent, of Warrington. By his will the parties' father gave his estate to ,his four children named in his will in equal shares. The plaintiff claimed as the testator's eldest son and heir-at- law to be entitled, in addition to the share given him by the will to the share given to the testator's daughter Mary Smith, who died a spinser, and intestate before the testator. Mr. Eastwood (instructed by Mr. A. Browne) appeared for the plaintiff, and Jr.A Maberley and Mr. Lawrence (instructed by Messrs. Robert Davies and Co.) for the defendants. After hearing the arguments of counsel the Vice Chancellor gave judgment, declaring that in the events which had happened the testator died mtestator as to the share of realty given to his daughter Mary Smith, and that the plaintiff became entitled to her one-fourth share of the realty in question as the testator's heir-at-law, and consequently was entitled to one half of the lands and hereditaments, the subject of the claim. His Honour also gave directions for the partition among the parties of the property in question in ac3ordtnce with the declaration. Asic for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINIMAL WATERS.—Advt. A Holiday in Rome. _ _

Mr. F. R. Roberts, M.A., L.L.8., gave a lecture last night in the Old Academy on a visit to Rome Aid by him and slme friends in the spring of, this yea. Mr. E. J. Hall was in the chair, awl there was a large attendance. The lecture was illustrated with about 100 lantern slides. Mr. Roberts sketched the journey from Calais through France and Switzerland into Italy, via the Mont Cenis Tunnel. A short description was given of the stay in Turin, which was described as a curious mixture of ancient and modern monks in their medieval garb, jostling mechanics in blue slops and carrying tin cans. Genoa and the even more famous Pisa were deScribed, and a sketch was also given of the wonderful country seen by the traveller from the railway—hills crowned with ancient towns or the ruins of solitary castles intermixed with vineyards and orange and lemon ' groves. The desolate and malaria-haunted Campazia, which was crossed at night in a fearful storm of lightening, the vivid flashes of which showed in ghastly outline the weird trees and hillocks with no sign of lrnman habitation,made a profound impression on all the travellers, and when a gleam lit up a broad band of yellow water, and an Italian passenger announced the Tiber, the sensation was almost over- whelming. Mr. Roberts then described his stay. in Rome, dwelling on the hisiorical scenes witnessed by the famous ruins of The Forum, The Capital, The Colliseum, and other well-known remains, the l tracks of medieval ecclesiasticism in the innumerable churches and mornasteries dating from those ,ages, the " palaces " of the turbulent and powerful nobility of bygone ages, and the gloomy and awful silence of the catacombs. Finally, the lecturer described modern Rome with its up-to-date hotels, trams, theatres, and other characteristics of modern cities, and sketched also the rise and growth of the present constitutional monarchy, concluding with a few notes upon the social and political outlook in Italy, and the relations of the civil government of the Vatican, which were vividly illustrated by the presence in Rome of President Loubet during the lecturer's stay there. Many of the slides were exceedingly beautiful, and a very pleasant evening was spent.—A hearty vote of thanks to the lecturer Concluded the proceedings.

div.head: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
TOWN COUNCIL DECIDE TO PROCEED WITH THE WORK.
The Oppasitiol of Messrs, Fainlough.

Notwithstanding the threatened opposition from various quarters, the Warrington Council at their monthly meeting on Tuesday evening decided by a majority of three votes to proceed with the widening of Warrington Bridge. The discussion was introduced by the MA.YOR moving the adoption of the following minutes of the General Purposes Committee :—" It having been reported that besides threatening to take proceedings against the Corporation, Messrs. James Fairclough and Sons, Limited, refused to sell to the Corporation a strip of land required for the support of the parapet of the proposed cantilever near their ware- house adjoining the bridge, and that opposition to the proposed cantilevers had been threatened from other quarters, and having in view the probable extensions of tramway services between Warrington and Northwich and Knutsford awl the South Lancashire tramways : Resolved, 'That the proposed widening of the, bridge be deferred.!"

Alderman ; cirroN seconded. Alderman SKETHuRsT moved an amendment that the committee's minutes be confirmed with the exception ot the resolution deferring the widening of Warrington Bridge. The MAYOR: We discussed the matter at the General Purposes Committee meeting. Alderman SMETHURST: We did. We have discussed it many times and we are going to have another do to- night. (Laughter.) He contended that there had been quite sufficient "dabbling" with the matter. He did not believe there would be more than one action to consider—and that was Messrs. Fairclough's. The Council had said all along that they would fight the matter and they ought to go on with the bridge, and not wait until the light railway came. (Hear, hear,) If the light railway pro-uoters wanted more accom- modation let them pay for it. Whether the bridge was erected or not the Council would have to pay Mr. Webster his commission. IF should like to ask the Town Clerk if he had had a letter from Mr. H. Fair- dough, builder, with reference to his contract.. The Tows CLERK: No but his solicitor came to see me this morning. Alderman SMETHURST: That will do for me.Cantinu- ing, the alderman said they would have to face another law-suit. The contractor, understanding that the work was to go on, had bought a pile driver and other things specially for the work. and a sub-contractor had already signed his contract. It was evident the Corporation were to be landed in a law-suit.

Councillor A. PEACOCK seconded. He understood that the difficulty now was that the cantilevers could not be carried on one side ten feet all along, but would have to be lessened at one end to Bft, 61n., because they could not buy a small piece of land. He believed it would cost the Council a " fine penny "to get out of the contract they had arranged for. The TOWN CLERK: I might say that Mr. Fairclough's solicitor admitted to me that he had no legal claim against the Corporation on the matter of the contract. Councillor PEACOCK : Only a moral claim,l suppose but at any rate we cannot get out of paying Mr. Webster his commission.
The TCTTN CLERK: We won't have to pay him the fa 11 amount.
Councillor PEACOCK : We shan't get out of it for much less than £3OO.

The MAYOR said that he wouldilike to show them why the matter should be deferred.% the first place they hai no money to carry it out and would have to go to the local Government Board,fand when they went there they must be quite certain what they did require. They must also be sure what land they could get. Messrs. Fair- dough declined to sell an inch of the land at their end, and that meant that the cantilevers could not be carried out properly on one side. The Local Govern- ment Board would not sanction the borrowing of money to carry on lawsuits, and the costs of any action that might have to be defended would fall upon the rates. The question was whether it was really wise to go on with the contract in the face of difficulties of this description. The matter would only be defet red until the difficulties were removed.

Councillor PEMBERT—ON- said he could not seriously believe that Messrs. Fairhurst would take action over such a trivial matter as eighteen inches of land. The AlAnton : They clam all the lot. It doesn't belong to the Corporation and we sill have to buy it from someone.

C3uncillor PENIBERTON: There was not a single word about this when it was brought forward before. Continuing, he said it was well within the recollection of people in Wavrington that the hoarding and staging on Fairclough's side had only been there a few years. If Messrs. Fairclough stood in the way of the town for the sake of 18 inches of land he thought it would be very unkind, especially considering that the Corpora- tion had bought a considerable amount of land from them and had given good prices for it and that the firm had had the advantage in several transactions with the Corporation. Still if Messrs. Fairclough commenced an action, the Corporation must fight them. The Council would not hesitate about going to arbitration with poor, insignificant ratepayers. He did not think the bridge widening ought to be shelved, even if they had to do without the 18 inches of land. Alderman SUTTON: Oh, yes; any sort of bridge will do.

-Councillor PEMBERTON : No, it won't. I sympathise with Messrs. Fairelough to a great extent and I shouldbe willing that something should be spent if necessary to improve the navigation of the river. I recognize that Messrs. Fairclough are large ratepayers and it is well for the industries of the town that the Corporation should in every way help the traders. I don't, however, think it is right for the Council to knuckleunder to big firms. We ought to go on with our business and do our duty to the ratepayers. Councillor WILKINSON : Our cantilever scheme will encroach upon Messrs. Fairclough's land for 18 filches, but there is the 8 feet or so of staging there, and Messrs. Fairclough 's right to that is only a possessive right. I want instructions given to the Town Clerk to challenge that right, and see if the requisite number of years have passel to establish it. (Hear, hear). If I remember rightly the old staging never did come up to the abutment of the bridge. The question is how many years the present staging has been up. Councillor BARTON said that had it not been for threats of actions by the Ship Canal Company, Admiral Nares, and Messrs. Fairclough, he believed the scheme would not have been deferred at the last committee meeting. The MAYOR :• Admiral Nares only wanted to see the plans to find out whether we were encroaching on his rights. He would not do anything until he was satis- fied that navigation would be impeded. Alderman BENNETT said he had never been in favour of a cantilever schetne as he had always thought it would be wisest in the long run to carry out a com- plete scheme at once. He must, however,enter his pro- test against this apparently new idea that because one particular firm had an interest in a public improvement that improvement must stand aide. It was a monstrous doctrine and should not be tolerated for a moment in this twentieth century. He thought it was quite time they put their foot down on the principle that the wel- fare of Warrington was higher than that of. any indi- vidual firm and ought to dominate the action of the Council. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BUTTON thought that in face of the diffi- culties put forth it was undesirable to proceed with the scheme until the whole matter had been further con- sidered. There were many important matters to be borne in mini, such as the widening of the road, and other work on the Latchford side of the river. Messrs. Fairclough were large ratepayers and considered the question so important that they were prepared to give a thousand pounds towards theerection of a new bridge. They said traffic under the bridge would be endangered and they were entitled to some consideration. Councillor WILKINSON: No more than me. It is my birthright. Alderman SurroN : I say there would be no barn in deferring the matter for a time. It would be simply throwing the money away if we spent £2,000 and then I found the bridge was not sufficient for our purpose. Councillor WILKINSON: It would last for fifty years. Councillor Trs-NroN said that as one of the sub-com- mittee which met Messrs. Fairclough he would say that Messrs. Fairclough would fight hard, and whether the Corporation won or lost, it would cost them a thousand or two. The matter was of so -much importance to the firm that they were prepared to fight the matter in every court in England. As to the question itself he thought that no matter that had ever been before the Council during his experience had been so stupidly dealt with. Four times they had decided to widen the bridge and they had not starred it yet, something having cropped up each time. If Messrs. Fairclough could get the bridge and the naviga- tion improved they were perfectly justified in using every fair and legitimate means to do so. He believed Messrs. Fairclough and others who navigated the river had so much influence with the Conservators that Admiral Nares was prepared to oppose the widening by cantilevers on the west side at any rate. As the matter now stood they were certain of Messrs. Fairclough opposing; there was a probability of the Ship. Canal Company opposing; and it was almost certain that Admiral Nares would oppose. Under the circumstances, therefore, he did not' think it was wise to go on with the scheme. He suggested that some limit—say two onth—should be placed on the period of deferring. h The MAYOR said he had no objection to giving sue an undertaking, but he certainly thought the schem? , should be deferred, on financial grounds alone. Firs' I the contract was £3,500. That amount borrowed, at six per cent, for sinking fund and interest would mean about £2lO a year. If the law costs and incidenta expenses came to £2,000 that sum would have to be levied on the rates so that the first year or two they would have the law costs to pay as well as the £`4o a year. The cost of making the half of a new bridge, as previously suggested, would be £7,000, of which Messrs. Fairclough would give £l,OOO, leaving £6,000 to be ' provided for, which would only mean £369 a year sink- ing fund and interest.
ouncillo r TINNION : Messrs. Fairolough would only

give us £l,OOO on the undertaking that we commenced to pull down Warrington Bridge in a very short time. The MAvoR said that even apart from Messrs. Fair- dough's £l,OOO they would only have to pay a thousand a year for two or three years until they got down to the ordinary level of interest, &c., and they would be on the way for a really good bridge instead of a dog leg affair. If they decided to defer the scheme he would see that it was brought up at the next meeting. Councillor TINNIO37 said Messrs. Fairclough were quite as strongly opposed to the building of half a new bridge as to the cantilevers.

Alderman HUTCHINSON thought it would be better to defer the matter for two months to enable the Corpora- tion to apply to the Local Government Board for the money required for the extension. The scheme should also be submitted to Admiral ares, on behalf of the Mersey Conservancy Board. Councillor BURTON was opposed to deferring the matter any longer, and said it would be extremely un- fair to the ratepayers to pull the bridge down and build a new one. It was only to oblige one family, the Fair- dough family, that an effort was being made in that direction. At the same time he had every respect for the Fairclough family. Alderman SUTTON : You must not take for granted all you hear. Have your own judgment. Councillor TINNION : All the manufacturers at that end of the town use the river. Councillor BURTON: Why have not the plans been deposited?
the M&YOR : The plans cannot be carried out unless we have the land.

Councillor BURTON: We are not going to bow down to people in this way. If they object, let us put a bridge over the river at Arplev. It would be a great convenience to the people of Warrington. The MAYOR: That would cost £17,000. Councillor BURTON suggested that the plans be de- posited with the Local Government Board. Councillor LORD said that if Messrs. Fairclough ob- jected to cantilevers they would object to half a bridge. Nothing to his mind would satisfy bhem but taking the pillars out, or taking the bridge away altogether, leav- ing the people to get over the river as best they could. (Laughter.) The best thing the Corporation could do would be to go cap in hand to Messrs. Fairolough and say "We will do whatever you want." (Renewed laughter.) Alderman PISRPOINT thought it was hardly fair to say that the improvement was only for the benefit of Messrs.Fairclough. That was not quite the right spirit to show. The advantage would be for all who had property above the bridge. The Corporation had land there for storing sets and all kinds of material, and they would benefit. Let them be fair on the whole question. He did not bold a watching brief for Messrs. Fairclough, but if the Corporation had a single-span bridge and freer access from Liverpool to their own stone yard, it would be a benefit to them as well as to Messrs. Fairclough. (Elear,hear.) He had always been in favour of widening by c mtilevers, and although he was strongly opposed to dictation from any private firm, he thought no harm could be done by deferring the matter for two months.

Councillor thoughtßßOTZlG-- Messrs. Fairclough had bad every consideration, and to his mind undue con- sideration. Had it not been for considering them the bridge would have been almost built by this time. If the bridge was somewhat spoiled by Messrs. Fairclough depriving them of the piece of land it would be to the firm's everlasting disgrace The voting was proceeded with as follows : POR THE AMENDMENT. AGAINST. Alderman Smethurst The Mayor " Francomb Alderman Bennett Councillors Barton „ Sutton Pf A- Peacock „ Pierpoint P. Peacock ~ Hutchinson Roberts „ Evans f t Wilkinson Councillors Cie zg ff Barton ' If Craik Ashcroft ' ft Fulton Smith PP Skelland IP Stott Wilson Wright ~ Benson f f Hulse „ ‘ Lord ff Tinni2n-13. ff Pemberton ff Brough 1 f Ellison-16. • The effect of the passing of the amendment is that the work be proceeded with. A further amendment by Councillor MINION that the matter be deferred for two months was allowed to drop.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

Coming Events. In connection pith the National Waifs and Strays Association a meeting ‘vill be held in the Co-operative Hall, on Friday next. Miss E. M. Rice (Warden of the Young Helpers' League) will give an address on " Slum life in our great cities" Mr. C. Jackson Holmes will preside. The annual choir festival in connection with Bold- street Wesleyan Church, will be held to-morrow and Monday. The principal feature will be the presenta- tion on Monday night of Mendelssohn's " Elijah." The preacher at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church to-morrow morning will be the Rev. J. Manning, and in the evening the Rev. J. Gunnell will occupy the pulpit. The sermon at Wycliffe Church to-morrow evening will be delivered by the Rev. J. Yonge, and will appeal specially to young people. An open meeting will be held in the afternoon in connection with the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society, at which the speaker will be the Rev. H. Cooke.
An open meeting of the Warrington P.S.A. Society will be held to-morrow afternoon. The speaker will be the Rev. F. Vaughan, and the soloist Afiss Polly Houghton.
XMAS PRESENTS.-Try J. S. GARLAND'S, 51 to 55, Bridge-street,Warrington.Splendid selection.—Advt. Personal.

The Bishop of Chester has appointed the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar of Frodsham, to the Rural Deanery of Frodsham in succession to the Ven. Archdeacon Maitland Wood, M.A. The Rev. T. Lee Jones has been offered and has accepted the living of All Saint's Church, Daresbury, recently vacated by the Rev. F. Clifton Smith. Mr. Jones at present is the headmaster of Guisborough Grammar School, Yorkshire. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS.—Advt. A Correction. In our report of the Hill Cliffs Baptist Church annual tea last week, we printed the name of Hr. Longland as the deliverer of a speech, whereas the speaker was really Mr. EaglAnd. Mr. Longland was not present at the gathering in question.
PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt.

Local Musical Successes. At the recent examination held at Liverpol November 2Sth and 29th in connection with the Victoria College of Music, London, the following pupils of Miss Annie Hill A.V.C.M., 6, Napier-street, Warrington,passed most creditably. Associate : Miss Mary Mills, Master Robert Hanson, and Master Percy Moores. This will entitle them to affix to their names the letters A.V.C.M., also to wear the Cap and Gown of the College. Intermediate Grade : Evaline Butter- worth, honours; Catherine Rowland, honours. Primary: Harold Homey, nhonours. Special mention may be made of Miss Mills who is only fifteen years of age and has gained honours for Associate *Grade.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
People's Services.

The Rev. H. Dannico continued the series of people's services at the Parr Hall on Sunday. when he again addressed a crowded congregation. His sermon was the last of three on "Immortality" his subject being "Shall we know each other beyond the grave." Madame Christian cave an effectively sung sacred solo. Next Sunday Mr. Einnnico will preach on "England's crime, socially, politically, morally, and religiously."

div.head: United Gathering.
div.p: United Gathering.

A united service was held in St. Peter's Church on Sunday, of the members of the Warrington P.S.A. Society,and the St. Peter's Men's Service. The members of the P.S.A. Society walked in procession from the Co-operative Hall, headed by the Pioneer Band. Mr. T. S. Steel presided, and the address was delivered by Rev. R. James, who gave a hearty welcome to the P.S.A. members. His subject was divided into three heads, the Living Christ, Living Word, and the Living Church. The soloists were Miss Bridge, who sang "Children asleep" and "I know that my Redeemer liveth" and Mr. Arthur Griffiths, who rendered "The Good Shepherd" and "The Star of Bethlehem." The deputy organist. Mr. F. Webster, gave an organ solo. The offertory was in aid of the Church Missionary Society.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

The usual meeting was held on Sunday, when there was a good attendance. Mr. T. L. Robins presided, and spoke i upon "The true standard of man's conduct." Mr. W. H. Shawcross, of Manchester, was the speaker. In.the course of his address he said the higher nature of man, developed, took him further away from all that was evil and degraded, and lifted him up and made him more like his Maker, with all the beauties of his 'Maker's oharacter—love, purity, and peace. We were fettered by environments, but that was only when we allowed environments to conquer, which ought not to be,as we had within us the power to conquer. By our efforts and the grace and power of God, our free wills should be sanctified to God's glory and service, which was our responsibility. The interest of the brethren were rivetted thoroughly by the speaker's addreas.—Mr. Farrar, the hon. sec., wel- comed two new members, and also referred to the death of Mr. Porritt, proposing that the deepest sympathy be sent to the widowand family. Mr. Joseph Hawthorn also took part in the service, and Mr. B. Hibbert was the soloist. Mr. Payton, Mus. Ba,c., presided at the organ.

Methodist Missionary Meeting. Mr. C. E. Parker Appeals for Greater Unity. The annual missionari meeting in co nnecti 311 with the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church was held on Tuesday evening when a fairly large congregation assembled at the Church. The Rev. R. Wilkins Rees read the report of the work done on behalf of the Wesleyan Missionary Society during the past year by the members of Bewsey- road Church, the report being in every way satisfactory. Mr. C. E. PARKER, who presided, spoke of the union in missionary work of the Evangelical Free Churches of Italy with the Wesleyan body. There was, he said, no truth which needed to be impressed upon the people more than that in our foreign work all Christians should be one, and that we should not in our endeavours to Christianise the world try to re-erect the somewhat flimsy divisions which separated Christian Churches at horn% Heiwas glad to recognize that in the foreign ' mission fields, although we might have our little differ- ences, the different societies were united in an active co-operation in accomplishing the great end of every ' Christian Church, the winning of the world for Christ. He often felt that at home a great deal of Christian energy and power was lost by our divisions and wished that in more ways all the Churches could unite upon those objects which Were common to all of them. If we could only see things in their true proportion and realize the smallness of the things which divided us and the greatness of the things which should unite us we would recognize that there should be more co-operation in the attaining of the great purpose for which Christian Churches were founded. (Hear. hear.) Mr. Parker quoted a portion of a speech recently delivered by the Bishop of Manchester in which greater unity among the churches in the mission fields and at home was strongly advocated. When we found a Bishop of the Church of England expressing such broad views, said Mr. Parker, he was sure we should respond and do all that lay in our power to bring about that expressed desire. Missions to foreign countries had lately been severely criticised, but in spite of what the critics urged against missions we could always fall back upon the fact that there was no other power whereby a man could be lifted from sin and sorrow,and whereby every man,no matter of what nationality, could be brought to Christ.(Applause) The Rev. C. FENELEY, a missionary from West Africa, delivered a very interesting address on the work in the mission field with which he was connected. He urged that we should all recognize the important part which individuals took in the salvation of the world. The reason why the Kingdom of God was such a long while in coming was that we had failed in ogr duty in trying to .influence others.
A collection was on behalf of the Missionary Society, a handsome sum being realized.

A cat which was taken from the house of a stud groom of the Duke of Beaufort, at Petty France, near Badminton, to Oakham, Rutland, escaped after being in its new home a couple of days, and arrived at its old Gloucestershire home eight days afterwards, having travelled 800 miles. The Duchess of Beaufort verifies the story.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
WRETCHED HOME LIFE.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, before Air. R. T. Fairclough, and 'other magistrates, Albert, Moss Dobson, 20,Egerton-terrace, Powell-street, Latch- ford, was summoned for assaulting his wife, Mary Dobson, on November 28th.—Complainant said that on the date named defendant drank several bottles of whisky, smashed a lamp and was "raving mad." At -two o'clock in the morning he turned her out of bed and struck her three times in the mouth and face, causing much blood to flow. She left the house to look for the police, and walked to a friend's house for safety at Stockton Heath with only her nightgown and a wrap on. She had to sleep out for four nights,being afraid to stop with him.—She was married to defendant •in August at Lostock Gralam, and had been assaulted on three occasions since. He had almost ruined her and she had "never lived in such a hell before." He would not go to any place of worship and the language used to her children was "not fit for cattle to hear." He had not worked to her knowledge for the last four years.—Defendant denied the assault—The Chairman said the Bench considered the assault was an aggravated one and defendant would be lined 40s. and costs (£3 is. in all). They granted the wife it separa- tion order with 12s. a week alimony.

div.head: THEFT FROM THE BARRACKS.
div.p: THEFT FROM THE BARRACKS.

Thomas Sharpies, a militiaman, was charged at the Warrington Police Court on Monday with stealing a canvas coat and pair of trousers from a kit bag at Orford Barracks. Daniel O'Loughlan, Back Dallam- lane, was charged with receiving the stolen goods.— The Chief Constable stated that the suit was left safe by a private named Mackintosh in his kit bag at the barracks and was subsequently missed. Detective Clough saw the two prisoners talking together and questioned O'Loughlan as to what he had get under his coat. O'Longhlan produced the canvas suit and said Sharpies had given the articles to him to sell. The men had no right to the clothes which were Government -property.—Sharples said Mackintosh asked him to sell the suit for him as he was short of money.—O'Loughlan said that when spoken to by Detective tlongh he was holding the suit whilst Sharpies lit a cigarette.—Both prisoners were fined 10s. and costs,or in default 14 days imprisonment with bard labour.

div.head: PETTY PILFERIEG.
div.p: PETTY PILFERIEG.

Elizabeth Ann Rowlands, School-brow, was charged at:the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday with three thefts of clothing, the property of Mrs. Hough- ton, Mersey-street.—Superintendent Monaghan pointed out that the articles of clothing were missed on different dates, and it had been ascertained that the prisoner had pawned them.—Prisoner, who had been previously con- victed, was sent to gaol for three months with hard labour.

• A POINT WHICH FAILED. At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, James Andrews, a former Warrington footballer, was sum- moned for being in arrears of maintenance Lei to the Guardians of £s.—Mr. Knowles, solicitor, apAred for defendant, and explained that the defendant was ordered to contribute 3s. 6d. per week towaxds the maintenance of his mother, who was in the asylum. Mr. Knowles took several points upon which he urged that the order against the defendant could not be &forced, maintain- ing that a son could not be forced to contribute whilst the husband lived. In that case the husband and two sons had each been ordered to pay 3s. 6d. per week, a total of 10s. 6d., whereas the cost to the Guardians was only 9s. 4d. per week. He maintained that the order could not be enforced, as the Guardians had no right to make a profit out of the defendant, his brother and father. Mr. Shearer argued that the order was perfectly valid and the magistrates declined to make any alteration and ordered the defendant to continue the payment of 3s. 6d. per week and to pay in addition is, a week towards the arrears.—John Andrews, father of the first defendant, was then summoned for a similar offence and was ordered to pay off the arrears of £8 at the rate of 6d. per week.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court,
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court,
Minor Cases.

MONDAY—Before the Mayor (ia the chair). Alderman th Smeurst, Councillors. Wilkinson and Thornton, and Messrs. Pilling, W. Roberts and Wright. TREFT.—Edwin Horrabin, 31, Cartwight-street was charged with staining 16 yards of calico value ss. the property of the St. Helens Cable Com- pany.—lt appears prisoner was seen by P.C. Lewis carrying the calico and when questioned admitted he had stolen it.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.

Joint Harriers Run. The Sankey Harriers, Latchford Harriers and Bewsey-road Y.M.A. Harriers held a joint meeting on Saturday,starting from the Longford Hotel. The trail was laid over about 51 miles across Winwick-,Padgate and Orford by Messrs. Taylor, Waring, Farmer and Rowson, and the result was declared an easy victory for Sankey, who beat Latchford by 43 points, and Bewsey by 94 points. Details: Sankey Harriers ; Joseph Riley, 1 ; John Riley, 3 ; L. Edwardson, 6 ; E. Bothwell, 7 ; T. Minshull, 8 ; F. Mahoney, 9 ; total, 34. Latchford Harriers : 1, Green, 1 ; L Beckett, 5; J. Win- stanley, 33 ; total, 128.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, December 10, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 10, 1904.

rxr tiny I met nun again, or ratner But to my surprise, instead of taking off his cap and smiling and making the most of yesterday's acquaintance, he glared and plunged round the first crooked corner. Could this be a new kind of tactics ? I asked myself. Could it be that he wished to rouse interest by piquing curiosity ?

1 smiled with scorn at the thought, and deter- mined to shew the man at the first opportunity how futile were his subtleties. Still, if it were his object to make me think of him, I must confess that to a certain extent he succeeded, for it was a novelty to be glared at by a man, and the picturs of the big, brown, frowning fellow lingered in my wind.

That very evening my opportunity came. V afternoon walks had usually to be taken alone, as' Mrs. Pendennis's working days were long. I was' strolling by the sea at the sweet hour when the east is misty silver with the rising of the moon, the west fading pink with the setting of the sun. There he was, presumably lyinc, in wait, so I glared, and turning round marched away. But something seemed to force toe to glance back—just a fleeting glance, yet long enough to see that aiu man was standing off in the opposite direction. So far had he gone already that I was afraid he must have missed tuy protest.

For an entire week we kept it up. There were nqt many different walks to take, so it _need. not have been surprising that we almost invariably met. But as invariably we turned upon our tracks and—often met again. I could not help wondering who he was and all about him, and whether, after all, he really was one of them. Lifter a whole fortnight I came in from a walk one day to find Mrs. Pendennis nervous and embarrassed. "I've a confession to make, dear," she said at dinner. "Do forgive rue, but—l've let out to the vicar's wife—she called while you were out—who you really are. I'm afraid she's rather a gossip, and probably half Clovelly knows by this time."
"If by half Clovelly you mean the man," I retorted, "it doesn't much matter, for if he came for the purpose we suspect he must have known all along." "Don't say we suspect,' Margot. I don't suspect."

"Yon did. You know you did. If you don't now it must be because you've found out some- thing." "Well, I told you the dear vicar's wife was inclined to gossip, and her husband is an old acquaintance of the man's. That, she says, is what brought the man here. He wanted to find the quietest, most secluded spot in England, and he thought of his friend's description of Clovelly." "Why did he want a retired spot? Is he an escaped convict ? " "No. But his name is Cyril Cortellyon." "My goodness! Not the South African millionaire ?"

"Yes, dear. So it seems." "Why, he's got as much money as I have—more, perhaps." "That was his reason for wanting seclusion. You see, people made such a fuss about him on the Continent, where he travelled when he first came back from South Africa, and then when he returned to England it was just as bad. Girls behaved rather foolishly, and re—" "Oh, what fun. He ran away from them, too, and supposed that I was one of them, just as I've been supposing about him." "Very likely. But if the vicar's wife has repeated what I was indiscreet enough to let Out--"

"Then he knows by this time. I wonder—" But I didn't finish my sentence. I was wondering whether if we happened to meet in the morning he would avoid me again. We did happen to meet. I dropped a book— quite accidentally, of course. It fell into the water and he fished it out and gave it to me. He didn't glare, neither did I. It was no longer worth the trouble. Somehow we talked and we liked the same things. Besides, the common sorrow of being rich drew us together. I had never met a young unmarried millionaire before, and being with one aas wonderfully restful. By-and-bye it got to seem Ile nicest thing in the world. When he told me that I was the prettiest, sweetest girl he had ever seen I believed it, for he had nothing to gain by flattery. When he told me that he loved me I believed that, too, for he had twice as much money as he wanted, and the addition of mine would be a bore. He only liked me in spite of it. I believed him and he believed tue, and together we made the remarkable discovery )f how to be happy though rich. LTUE END.]
statement is very misleading, and that is a difficulty we constantly have to meet in this Council.

The MAYOR : Wait a minute. You are making charges that will want proving. The Town Clerk and the Mayor examined the estimates, the latter subsequently stating that the estimate said two engines, i&c., at a cost of .£12,000. They had put down an engine for .£ll,OOO, which was intended to do the work of the two 00 h.p, engines. Councillor PEMBERTON : But we cannot depend on that one large engine to supplyfa town. You are bound to have two. The MAYOR : A great many wells are worked with only one engine, and it is not many works where they have a big engine standing by doing nothing. Councillor PEMBERTON : IS it the intention of the Water Committee to put in the second engine? The MAYOR: It all depends on the water supply. I would never go and over-capitalize myself for the sake of having two engines when one would do the work. Councillor PEMBERTON IS it the intention of this committee to ask the Council to put in a second engine? What I object to is the whole of the Council not being taken into the confidence of the different committees, and I blame the Council as a whole arid every individual who votes for what he does not know anything about. The only safe way is for every public man not to vote if he'does not understand a thing. The MAYOR; I hope you never will. Councillor PEMBERTON : I won't. There are a great many men who don't perform their duty to the town, quite unintentionally, for the reason that it is perhaps made a little uncomfortable for them if they do. There in going to be a serious loss on this department and it ought to be faced manfully and straightforwardly as any ordinary business problem outside would be faced. The whole of this Council should be taken into the confidence of the comthittee, and if the Council would take my advice ther,would refuse to vote on this until they really understood the position. The MAYort : Will you move an amendment?

Councillor PEMBERTON : I move an amendment that until the Water Committee comes before this Council with a proper explanation of the amount of money required to complete this work, we do not pa s this minute. Councillor EVANS seconded.

The MAYOR: There is one thing I should like to explain. Two 90 horse power engines were provided for. The engine put down was 120 horse power. That is why there is only one instead of two. Councillor EvANs said that might be quite correct but in the absence of explanation as to why one power- ful engine was put down instead of two, that Council had a right to suppose, seeing that buildings were pro- vided for two engines that some day tho second engine would be put down. He thought the chairman of the Water Committee might have given the Council some further explanation as to why the £20,510 was wanted now, and what was proposed to be done with it. Councillor TIN-SioN : It's spent. Councillor EVANS.—No, no ; I take it that the money is not spent._ _ .

div.head: PERSONALITIES IN THE COUNCIL CHAMBER.
div.p: PERSONALITIES IN THE COUNCIL CHAMBER.
LIVELY DICUSSION ON THE WATER SCHEME.
MP_ _ MORE INFORMATION WANTED.

A lively discussion, culminating in a "scene" between Alderman Francomb and Councillor Pemberton, was engendered at the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening by the Water Committee's important proposals. It appears that the engineer bad submitted to the committee a statement showing the amount over- spent on the waterworks undertaking under the powers contained in the Act of 1899, and the further sum required to complete the works. It was resolved that the Town Clerk be instructed to apply to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of the sum of £20,510 for waterworks purposes. In moving the adoption of the minutes Alderman FRANCOMB pointed out that the total money they were authorized to borrow under the Act of 1899 was £147,000 They had completed the whole of that work almost exactly to the figures to which the estimates were worked out with the exception of the wells and tunnels at Winwick. Professor Boyd-Dawkins had estimated that they would have 1,200,000 gallons a day from the wells. Fortunately for them they were getting at least 3,000,000 gallons a day, so that for .L 147,000 they would have been content to have received only 1,200,000 gallons per day. The extra £20,510 would be incurred through having the excessive amount of water. They had had to pay a great deal of money for pumping, and it had seemed an almost impossible task to get through the work. They were nearly ithrough with the wells, and they expected to have them coupled up in a day or two. He had hoped to hear that evening that they had succeeded in making a way from one well to another. Mr. Fairhurst had a full statement to 3d. of what had been spent, and any member could see the details. He hoped they would pass the minutes, for although it was a rather large bill, they were compelled to finish the business, even if they had to spend another £20,000. Alderman EVANS seconded.

Councillor LORD asked whether provision had been made for two pumping engines in the original estimates, and whether if they bad not been supplied the 'money, i for them had been set aside, or was t Included in this £20,000? Alderman FRANCOMB said they had provided a build- ing for two engines, but it was only intended by the contract to purchase one. If they required another engine at any time they had the accommodation. Councillbr PEMBERTor: : In the Parliamentary powers you provide for two 90 horse power engines, and you have only put down one. The MAYOR: 'Mr. Deas says that in the Parliamen- tary estimates, buildings were provided for two, but only one engine was provided for. Councillor PEMBERTON : It says in the Parliamentary estimates, two 90 h.p. engines. The TOWN CLERK: The original scheme was to spend £252,000, and in that estimate there was provision for two engines. The estimate was reduced to £147.000, only one engine being provided for. Councillor PEMBERTON : That was another scheme and it had nothing to do withtheenginss. I think that!,

div.head: Alder-man FRANCONIB : It is to finish the scheme.
div.p: Alder-man FRANCONIB : It is to finish the scheme.

Councillor EVANS : But you say on the one hand that the money is not spent. This is one of the unfor- tunate things that happen again and again. If they wanted £20,510, he continued, it was the obvious duty of the committee to come to the Council before spend- ing the money, and not after it was spent. Alderman FRANCOMB (after a conversation with the Borough Treasurer) : I find that we have only spent a small proportion of it. Up to October 31st we were overspent £2,509 us. 2d., but it is a going concern, and we cannot stop in the work. Councillor EVANS said he did not remember hearing the Chairman of the Water Committee say anything as to what was going to be done with the extra money to be borrowed, and this time he thought with Councillor Pemberton, that the Water Committee should take the Council into their confidence and actually tell them their proper intention. If this sum was necessary to com- plete the work, then it was the duty of that Council to sanction the borrowing of it. .

Councillor TINNION -said he was in favour of the amendment. It was just possible that although sanction was obtained to borrow £147,000 for specific purposes it was not so spent, and a good deal had been spent on objects other than that for which it was intended. The BOROUGH TREASURER: Oh yes.

ao-u-n-c-illo-r-iiis7;r-o-N-,.-COniin-tiini,--stild-he did not think it was desirable or in the interests of the Corporation that they should have to discuss matters in Council with officials. They should have sufficient information plaeed before them when asked to discuss the questions in committee, and should not have to get their informa- tion piece-meal from the officials at the Council meet- ing. For the reason that he did not think they had sufficient information as to what the £20,510 was for, he supported the amendment. Councillor Pemberton asserted that a portion of that money had been got for certain purposes and spent for something else. It had been challenged that a sum was provided for two engines and only one was put down. If an engine of 120 h.p. was put down instead of two of 90 h.p. where was the balance of the money, and if spent where had it gone and for what purpose? The MAYOR said as far as he could gather £12,000 was provided for engines, and they had bought an engine at £ll,OOO, leaving a balance of £l,OOO. Instead of two smaller engines they put in the bigger engine in order to cope with the surprising quantity of water found, which rendered it useless to put a 90 h.p. engine down. The extra cost of £20,000 was one of those ex- penses which arose when a bargain turned out better than they anticipated, and the cost of sinking these wells was increased from the very fact that they had expected less than two million gallons a day, and instead they had perhaps four million gallons. If it cost a little bit more they could not grumble as they would have the better supply at the finish. . .

Councillor LORD asked 'if it was the intention of the committee to provide a duplicate engine or depend upon the one. He thought the sooner they had a duplicate the better. It was always customary to have a stand-by engine. Alderman Surrox suggested that the Chairman of the Water Committee should defer the question until the next meeting of the Council, so that they might have the full explanation as to what the money was required for. (Hear, hear.) %The MAYOR: You are spending the money. You are bound to pay your men. Councillor TrlmoN : £2,000 has been spent without sanction. Spend another few hundreds in the meantime. Alderman FRANCOMB: That is all we want. (Laughter.) He further explained that there was accommodation made for a second engine and whenever the committee were satisfied that it was required they would come to the Council for permission to purchase one. They must remember that they had also two other sets of engines at Winwick. He thought that they might ask Councillor Pemberton, who seemed to know everything, to give them a report on the matter. (Laughter.) Why in the world did he not find out these things at the committee ineeting,s when they could have the officials and figures before them and not go and spring the matter upon them like a mine? Councillor WILKINSON: Will you join Councillor Evans in that?

Councillor EVANS : I protest. The MAYOR : You are not a member. It is only a suggestion. Councillor EVANS : A very wild one. Alderman FRANCOIUB said it was unfair for Councillor Pemberton to come there in that way. He could get all this information at the meetings of the committee The extra expenditure was simply on account of the extra amountlof water the committee had to contend with, and they must go on or let the workings fill with water. The committee were at present sending 500,000 gallons per day to Hill Warren and they had also been sending the same quantity to the old reservoir. Had it not been for those measures the supply for manufactur- ing purposes would have been exhausted three weeks Councillor PEMBERTON : I must rise to explain. I must object to the observation that I can get all I want to know on the Water Committee. Alderman FRAWCOMB : Let him make these state- ments. He can get whatever he likes. Cofincillor PEMBERTON : I say I cannot. , Alderman FRANCOMB : You are telling a deliberate untruth. You ought to be ashamed of yourself. COUROiIIOT PEMBERTON made several attempts to speak, but was ruled out of order. He protested that he had a right to make an explanation. Councillor WILKINSON : Let him make an explana- tion, but not an accusation. If be accuses any official of withholding information I make the same reply as Alderman Francomb.

The MAYOR: You had better bring this matter up at the next committee meeting, Councillor Pemberton, and I will come personally and see fair play. co. uncillor PEMBERTON : I will bring a resolution be We the Council. I refute all that Alderman Fran- comb has said in regard to me. , Alderman FRANCOMB : You will refute anything if there is any truth in it.

div.p: OF
AND OTHER SIZES.
THE GIRL WHO WAS TOO RICH.
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.j
BY MRS. C. N. WILLIAMSON, author of "Lady Mary of the Dark House," "The Woman in are), " "The Barnstormers," "The Mystery Box," "Queen Sweetheart," &c.

Nobody who hasn't gone through it knows how horrid it is to be rich. I mean very rich—so rich that people say, "There goes the rich Miss Ellice." Not "pretty Miss Ellice, or "nice Miss Ellice," though it does seem to me that 1 have dome claim to both those adjectives, but always that inevitable "rich Miss Ellice." .

I was as nearly born an orphan as anybody could be, for my mother died when I was a day old and My father a few months later, leaving me with all those oppressive millions and no blood relations (I always hated that expression, it sounds so murderous) to look after me, so I was made a ward in Chancery. _ _ . _

My very nurses used to toady tO me, and as for the children I was allowed to know, several of them admitted regarding me as a kind of natural curiosity because I was 'an heiress." By the time that I was sent to boarding-school (it was a good way for my pastors and masters to get decently rid of the bother, of me for several years) I was fast becoming a 'misanthrope. The girls at school were lovely to me and so were the teachers, but I had never been able to forget the words of an angry playmate whom I had once adored and who had given me my first heartbreak.

"My mother says rm to be sweet to you because you're such a lonely little girl," my false friend had remarked. "But that isn't the reason really, it's because you're rich. Nobody'd be so good to you if you weren't rich, I heard my father say so, and that it'll be like that all your life. But I don't care. I'm tired of being sweet to you, and I shan't be any more."

I had a large allowance and I could do a good deal for the girls. They invited me to %isit them in the holidays, and I went because I had no real home quite my own to go to. And the girls' brothers invariably made love to me. I had more attention at dances than anyone else, and I might have enjoyed myself immensely if there hadn't been always that canker at my heart. I dared not take kindness or admiration for myself alone. There was always the remembrance of my wretched ,money, and I used to envy the poor girls who were \perhaps envying me. \ When I was nineteen a chaperon was engaged to live with me and travel about the world. ei had longed to travel, but I soon found out it was just as bad being abroad as in England. How the facts about me leaked out everywhere I don't know. I wanted to take a false name and have a'little peace, but my chaperon, who was a Bishop's widow, and rather rigid in her ideas, would not hear of "passing under false pretences" as she called it. If the truth were known I believe that Mrs. Do Selwyn in her quiet way enjoyed the kind of triumphal progress we made wandering about the Continent.

People never failed to find us out at hotels. Whispers and glances went round, and mothers with sons scraped acquaintance with us and were unpleasantly maternal. In Italy I was fairly mobbed with impecunious young noblemen and officers, and would have been amused if I hadn't been furious. In Germany it was much the same.. and in Paris I narrowly escaped being kidnapped. When I couldn't stand it any longer we went back to England. It was just at the beginning of the season, and Mrs. De Selwyn was determined that I should be presented. I was presented, and the inevitable consequences ensued. We took little house in Park-lane, and in the first month I had forty-eight proposals. By the end of the season I had quite lost count, and I was so sick of it all—so deadly sick, knowing only too well that not one of the men who had asked me to marry them would have dreamt of doing it if it had not been for my millions.

I could 'have been two duchesses—l mean, that two dukes were among the moths who burnt their wings at the golden lamp; and there was even a lesser royalty—but it seems like boasting to enumerate them; whereas, in reality, with each proposal I had one more point of my vanity was broken off until finally I had none left at all.

Things went on cn this way, growing worse instead of better, for two years. I felt old and blase, and had lost my faith in the disipterestedness of men and women. I was not intended by nature to be cynical, but experience was thwarting nature, and the people who made themselves so charming must often have disliked me intensely, though all the while I was starving for love—honest love without the suspicion of a mercenary twist. When 1 was twenty-one, and free—as much as a girl can be free—to do as 1 chose Mrs. De Selwyn and I had a quarrel. it was a silly quarrel about an equally silly ' young man, my chaperon's nephew, whom she'd been scheming for years, it seemed, to have me marry. I was so disgusted that I threw over a lot of country-house engage- ments and rushed off to the only person whose love had ever been proved to be for myself and not my money. She was a dear old proud thing, who wrote love stories for magazines, and had refused to accept a penny from me when she was threatened with consumption and had been sent away from London to Devonshire to live. She had taken a tiny cottage in Clovelly, for which she paid no more in a year than I spent for nothing at all in a week. But she had a spare room, and wrote that she would love to keep me for as long as I liked to stay. Her name was Mrs. Pendennis, and we had got acquainted through my writing, in care of her editor, to tell her how much I liked a story of hers. She did me good because she never flattered, but scolded me instead of being cynical. She said it was a "mental dyspepsia," and while I lived with her I almost believed it was.

I hadn't been in Clovelly for a week when one day I came in from a walk and exclaimed: "Well. it's begun!" "What has begun ? " inquired my dear old friend, looking up from a love scene which was meant to make the public shed tears. "The usual thing," said I. "A man has come. I am not conceited, but there are signs, and I'm sure he is one of them."
She knew what I meant without asking, and merely sat still with a mild smile as I related the incident which_had occurred. _

Circumstantial evidenie was with me, for men were out of season in Clovelly. I had been the only stranger. Now, within a week of my advent, there was another—a male stranger, a gentleman to the eye and ear, well dressed (but not too ‘well dressed), staying at a humble inn which offered no inducement at this time of the year to his kind. 1 had seen him come out of that inn, and instihct told me that I was the inducement. Who the man was I could not guess, but I was sadly sure that he more than guessed who I was. Somehow my secret had been betrayed, and he—no dcnbt of the army of impecunious ones—had stalked me to my lair. My hat had blown off, he had run after it, picked it up, and handed it back with a bow and a murmured word.

To be sure he had not followed up his advantage, but I was certain that this was only his cleverness, and that he would be more pushing next time. I was so hatefully experienced in that kind of thing —I knew all the phases. Mrs. Pendennis tried to cheer me up, but I had seen the speck in my garnered fruit, and it was a big speck, at least six feet tall and °road in prt.‘" portion. One couldn't forget it, esp.j an' tef a Jess sophisticated mind it might have appeared exceedingly good to look UDOD.

div.p: IS
"HEALTH" says
THE NEW SCHOOL FOR LATCHFORD. Councillor Pemberton Thinks the Price of Land "Monstrous."

A resolution of the General Purposes Committee in regard to the site of the new school at Latchford was the cause of some discussion at the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening. The committee had resolved on the recommendation of the Education Committee, that a plot of Land containing 12,436 square yards situate near Lower Wiksh-lane be purchased from Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., Ltd., for the site of anew school, at 4s. 9d. per square yard ; also that the Town Clerk be authorised to apply to the Local Govern- ment Board for their sanction to the borrowing of the sum of £2,953 lls, for the purchase of the school site in Latchford.

Councillor PEMBERTON moved an amendment that the recommendation be referred back to the committee. He pointed out that he had had considerable experi- ence in land purchasing in the Latchford district, in fact he knew of every transaction of the kind which had taken place during the past twelve years. The most expensive purchase did not come to half the price the Council was giving for the site of the new school. It was simply a monstrous price, and he earnestly appealed to the Council not to sanction the payment. If they were going to give that price for land in a country lane at Latchford what were the schools going to cost in Warrington where land was valuable? In that very neighbourhood he himself had bought land in a better position for building purposes from the same firm at less than half the price. It looked as if Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company han thought the Council would go to arbitration and had charged a high price thinking that it would be re- duced.
The MAYOR: Would you be surprised to know that they gave ss. per yard for some ofithe land they are selling at 4s. 9d? ... _..—.
COULlediOr PEMBERTON : They may have given it for a very small piece of la,nd in order to gain access to the plot.

I n reply to Councillor PEMBERTON, the MAYOR said that all children attending the school from outside the borough would be charged for. The present site was the only one the Board of Education would accept. Councillor PEMBERTON : Have you offered others to them?

The MAYOR: They have had sevesal. Councillor PEMBERTON submitted that the very out- side price of the land was £1,200. He would suggest that the Council make inquiries as to the price usually paid in the Latchford district. At the present rate, the sites for all the new schools would cost about £30,000. He said without fear of contradiction that the highest sum given in the property market for land in the Latch- ford district was £550 per acre. If Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company would not accept a more reason- able offer the Council,ought to adopt the same course that they took in the case of weaker people and go to arbitration.

The MAYOR: Some of you are very fond of law. Councillor PIiMBERTON said the Ship Canal Company and other owners were willing to sell land for much less than the amount asked by Messrs. Greenall,Whitley and Co.

Councillor ASHCROFT seconded the amendment. The MAYOR pointed out that a number of farm build- ings would have to be removed from the site and rebuilt, and taking that into consideration, as well as the situa- tion of the land and the purpose for which it was required, he did not think the price was any too dear. If the Council did not sanction the purchase theewere going to lose the Government grant for the district of about £1,200 a year. The Government Inspector had visited Warrington that day and asked him to inform the Council that if things were not more seriously taken up, he would advise a Government inquiry and that would cost the Council a great deal as the effect would probably be that they would have to build a number of temporary schools. Councillor ELLISON said he wished to correct Coun- cillor Pemberton as to the prices in the Latchford district. He happened to be the trustee of 100 yards of land in the neighbourhood which was purchased ten years ago at 3d. per yard mote than the Council was giving for the present site. Councillor PEMBERTON said he was talking of acres, not yards. Alderman SUTTON said he was afraid Councillor Pem- berton was unfortunately rather prejudiced against Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. The question was: Were the Council getting the right piece of land, and where they pitying the proper ;price for it? Although Councillor -Pemberton had no doubt had a great deal of experience in the purchasing and selling of land, he (Alderman Sutton) might also claim to have some knowledge of the value of land. He was of oPinion that if the site in question was suitable for the purpose, the price was not dear at all. In many cases the erection of schools was regarded as a detraction from the value of surrounding property, and therefore more had to be paid for the land.

Councillor BURTON said he had thought the price was altogether too high, but the explanation in regard to the rebuilding of farms altered the case materially. Councillor STOTT thought the price was high but it appeared to him that there was no way out of the diffi- culty. The Corporation would have to pay a very high price for all land they required in Warrington. Through municipal enterprise the value of land was enhanced to those who did not contribute a penny towards its in- creased value. The whole of the land in the town ought to belong to the ratepayers. Alderman BENNETT said he had much sympathy with what Councillor Stott had said but the subject was too large to discuss that night. On the immediate question he was inclined to agree with Councillor Pemberton that they were paying a very stiff price, but they were in a difficulty. The site was the only one which ap- peared to be suitable and the matter was one of the greatest urgency. He did not think the Council would

Diagram 34 shows a series of run-throughs into a baulk pocket. The red ball being on the baulk line and. touching the side cushion and the cue ball at A being on a spot 12 inches to the left of the pyramid spot (looking down the table to- wards baulk) at B on a spot six inches to the left of the pyramid spot, at Con the pyramid spot and at I), E, F, and G on spots respectively 6, 12, 18 and 24 inches to the right of the pyramid spot, and in every case on a line straight across the table passing through the pyramid spot. From each position of the cue-ball the run- through in-off can be made without any, side simply by the use of top and strength. In fact, the best way of playing the in-off from the several positions is by a strong plain full ball stroke with plenty of top. In each case the •object ball must be hit quite full, and the only difficulty in the stroke is hitting the ball full when playing at high speed. Many players find a greak difficulty in hitting a distant ball quite full when playing a strong stroke, a" the strength of the stroke destroys their aim. Accurate strikinc, is, however, far easier when playing a plain 'ball stroke than when playing with side. When playing the stroke from A or B in the manner I have described, high speed is not absolutely essential, though a fast stroke must be used each time the cue ball is placed more and more to the right of the table. When the cue ball is at E, F or G only an extremely high-pace stroke can be successful, and the in. off is therefore quite beyond the power of any player who has not very great power of cue.
