div.head: ROBERTS v. BATEMAN MATCH.
div.p: THE ROBERTS v. BATEMAN MATCH.

Throughout the whole week Roberts played in magnificent form, reaching three figures on no less than twenty-seven occasions. Seven of the breaks were over two hundred, as follows, 209, 211, 220, 231, 240, 269, and 276, and Roberts also made a great break of 595. This break is Roberts's record under the new rules, his previous best having been 584 in a match with Steven- son at the Egyptian Hall,London in March of 1900. It only shows what a marvel Roberts is in that he stiould make his record break in his 58th year. To those who were fortunate enough to see Roberts play in his previous matches this season this great break did not come as a surprise, for Roberts all through the month of November displayed such wonderful form that one had not to be much. of a prophet to foretell that he would be making some very big breaks before long. In my6otes on Roberts v. Reece, written three weeks ago, I stated that Roberts would in all proba- bility make a 500 break before the year was out, and I hadvnot to wait long before my prediction came to pass. Had Roberts not reached his points on the Tuesday night with 593 unfinished he most likely would have very considerably increased the break. Big unfinished breaks are seldom increased very much the next session. Stevenson's great break of 703, made last year, may be cited as an example. When he had made 687 he had reached his points, and the balls were left in perfect position at the top of the table, yet he only added 16 at the next session. With Roberts also the balls were in good position at the top of the table, when he resumed his break. He potted the red, but played the stroke too slowly, and left his ball near the ton cushion about 9 or 0 inches from the corner pocket. The in-off which he then played into die opposite cornerlpoc,ket was an ex- ceedingly difficult stroke (in many papers it was termed a comparatively easy in-off), only to be got by a strong forcing stroke—a very unreliable stroke in this position —or by a half-massd stroke made by raising the butt of the cue and aiming full at the red ball with running side. When such a stroke is well played the cue ball though aimed full on to the red swerves in its path and catches the red half ball, and the swerve causes the cue ball to run on to the red from what is more or less a natural angle path. The difficulty in the stroke lies in gauging the amount of swerve and though Roberts during the month he was playing in Manchester time after time played this particular stroke with wonderful precision and ease, on this occasion caused his ball to swerve a little too much, with the result that the red was caught too thinly to allow the in-off being made. This 595 break is the highest break made this season, in fact no one else at the time of writing has yet made a 500 break, and though in all probability it will be beaten more than once during the season, Roberts is quite as likely to beat it as any other professional.

div.p: ANSWERS TO CORRESPONDEArS.

H. Bentley (Salford).—Roberts was bot:n in Man- chester in August, 1847. "R. C. D." (Marple).—The Badminton book on Billiards was first published at 10s. 6d., but a cheaper edition was published sometime afterwards at 6s.

T. W. Sinclair (Finchley).—l can Cquite understand that you can go from ivories to crystalates and vice versa, with little or no difference to your play, and this is accounted for owing to the throw-off angle of crystalates being practically the same as with ivories in all except forcing strokes. If you watch Stevenson's performances you will find that one week he plays with crystalates, and the next with ivories, and so on, and yet changing from one ball to another appar- ently makes no difference to his play. Take InmanaTho, look how well he played with ivory balls in his match with Roberts (in one break he made 162 off tip red ball !), and yet for two or three weeks previously hehad been playing with crystalates. Players like Stevenson and Inman when playing with ivory balls always have a reliable set to play with, but in hotels and clubs far more often than not ivory balls are very unreliable. In your own case unless you have a very good set of ivory balls I think you would be very well advised to stick to orystalateo. le. Bentley (Halifax.)—When playing the game in a tournament handicap, if it be found that the balls are over-size—and 2* balls are oversize—either player has a Tight to object to the balls. If, however, a few minutes after the game has commenced both players are aware that the balls are oversize, but notwithstanding this they continue the game and finish it,the loser can- not afterwards raise any objection to the balls. Such a state of affairs would be outrageous; it would tie tantamount to a player saying tp himself, "I will play the game out, if I win, well and good; if I lose, I will raise an objection to the balls." Even if your opponent raised an objection at the time the same could not be upheld, as he finished a game. The gamemust therefore stand as a win to you.

div.head: ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING.
div.p: ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING.

At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Tuesday, G before Mr. F. A. Frost, Thomas Barrago, rafton-street, Earlestown, was charged with unlawfully wounding his wife, Mary Barrago, on November 21st.—Complainant said her husband came home on the aftermion of the date named about two o'clock under the influence of drink. Later he went into his next door neighbour's house, occupied by Mrs. O'Malley, and a few minutes afterwards she heard quarrelling, and on going to see what was the matter, she found her husband, Mrs. O'Malley and her daughter struggling on the sofa. Mrs. O'Malley had a poker in her hand. Witness asked her husband to return home, but he struck her two violent blows, which " dazed " her. Directly afterwards he struck her on the left side of thehead with a poker, and she fell against the wall, and then returned to her house the best way she could. Her head was bleeding and she was in great pain.—Dr.Valentipe,arlestown, described the nature of Mrs. Barrago's injuries. The same blow, he said, a couple of inches forward would have proved fatal.—Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
NORTHERN LEAGUE.
First Division.
WARRINGTON v. WIDNES.

This interesting local fixture came off at Warrington on Saturday, both sides being at full strength. Hocken- hall resumed his position at half for Warrington,for the first time since his injury in the County match with Yorkshire. The weather was again fine and the turf in good order, and about 5,000 people assembled. Teams and officials :

Warrington—Hallam, back; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son and Harris, threequarter backs; D. Davies, and Hockeuhall, half backs; Preston, Boardman, Shugars, Thomas, Naylor, Jolley, Cook, and Bilton, forwards. Widnes—Tilley, back; Wailing, I. Taylor, Peacock, and Gill, three-quarter backs ; A. Taylor and Lolly, half backs; S. Aspey, Lynch, McDonald, McCabe, Webster, Rigby, Argent, and Cockram, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Priestley, Broughton Rangers; touch judges, Messrs. J. Worrall (Leigh), and J. Edwards (St. Helens). Widnes started, and the opening phases of the match went in favour of the home men, Fish and Harris making futile attempts to cross at their respective corners. Capital defensive work was exhibited by Tilley, and subsequently a strong run gave Hallam trouble. By degrees Warrington again resumed the offensive, and eventually Preston had a successful shot from a penalty. The leaders now forced the pace, and a clever concerted movement, in which Davies and Fish were the prime movers, resulted in a try to the former. Widnes failed at an easy shot at goal, and at half-time Warrington led by 5 points to nil. For a time in the second half the game was even, but by degrees Warrington took up a strong attacking posi- tion, and Preston recorded his second penalty goal. Widnes next hada turn of pressing, and the two Taylors reached the Warrington line in a capital movement. Fish drove out the invaders, and after Hallam had been fouled, for which Rigby received marching orders, Fish landed a third penalty goal. Final: Warrington, 3 goals, 1 try (9 points), 'Widnes, nil.

div.head: RUNCORN v. OLDHAM.
div.p: RUNCORN v. OLDHAM.

The visit of the League leaders attracted an attend- ance of about 2,000 spectators at Runcorn. Half-time arrived with the score-sheet blank. The second half opened in favour of the visitors, and following a scrum- mage in the home half, Dixon got possession and dropped a/goal for Oldham. Runcorn then attacked, but another fine run by Cash brought relief, and from a mark Ferguson placed a goal. Immediately on resump- tion the same player added another goal from a mark. A desperate attack by Runcorn then followed, scrum- maging taking place near the Oldham posts. The visitors were penalised, but Price failed to place a goal. Re- suming. Oldham attacked, and Ferguson had another attempt at goal, but without success. The remainder of the game was evenly contested. Result—Oldham 3 goals (6 points), Runcorn nil.

HULL vt ST. HELENS. This match, which wal played on the Hull Boulevard, may be summed up briefly as a poor display. Hull started, and seemed like doing great things as soon as the ball was kicked oft. Cook was within a stride of ;the line when he was tackled, and almost immediately Good- fellow kicked a penalty, goal, a f at which he repeated before half-time was called, with Hull leading by four points to nil. Hull made a spurt towards the finish, when Freer scored near the post, and Jenkins added another in an equally good place. Both tries were converted by Goodfellow. Result :—Hull 4 goals and 2 tries (14 points), St. Helens nil.

div.head: LEEDS V. WICPAN.
div.p: LEEDS V. WICPAN.

The Leeds team met with something in the nature of a shock on Saturday, being beaten on their own ground by Wigan. It was a pleasant day for football, and about 10,000 spectators turned up to witness a fairly exhilarating struggle. At the end of the first five minutes a scrummage was formed at the Wigan " 25," and Mosley getting the ball, passed to Thomas. The old Oldham man drew• hislopponents .very cleverly before passing to Llewellyn, and the latter had a clear run in as a consequence. Littlewood crowned a pretty com- bined movement by placing an easy goal. Just before the interval the scene was changed in a remarkable manner. The ball was being passed among the Leeds backs, when Leytham rushed in, got his toe to the ball, and kicked the oval up the field. He followed up and retained poSsession of it, and having a clear field, gave a fine exhibition of \ speed and scored an easy—though clever—try, to which Mason added a goal. Thus at the interval the sides were level on the score-sheet with five points each. From Mosley's restart a rush by the Wigan pack was similarly responded to by the Leeds eight, but the Lancastrians were soon scrummaging again!at the Leeds "25." The Wigan men got in front on the score-sheet in a somewhat similar manner to the incident that led to the first score. Breaking up a woefully slow passing movement among the Leeds backs, the Wigan backs followed up the ball after kicking it down the field, and Leytham picking up, was able to again out-pace all opponents, and score a grand try. Mason placed a goal The whistle sounded for "no-side" in semi-darkness Wigan running out the winners by 2 goals 2 tries (10 points), to a goal and a try (5 points).
WAKEFIELD v. HUNSLET : TRINITARIANS WIN A KEEN GAME.

One of the keenest struggles seen for a long time on the Belle Vue ground at Wakefield, was that between Wakefield Trinity and Hunslet, as right up to the sound- ing of the final whistle the issue was in doubt. Bennett succeeded in establishing Wakefield in an attacking position, where Newbould secured the ball from the pack, and sent it sailing over the bar. The home team were not long, however, before they lost the lead. From a scrummage in the home quarters Albert Gold- thorpe received possession, and passed to Bentley, who in turn transferred to Walter Goldthorpe. The latter rushed over in irresistible fashion,sconng a try, which he was also successful in improving with a goal. Hars- let continued to act on the aggressive until the interval, when they changed over three points ahead.

The Wiketlea forwards asseited themselves early on ' in the second half, and for a prolonged period they kept Hunsiet pinned to their own line. Bennett, after re- ceiving a long pass from Newbould romped over and scored a splendid try. Metcalfe failed with the shot at goal, and it look ed as if the match was going to end in a draw, when just in the last minute Jacques landed a winning goal for Wakefield from a penalty. R esult : Wakefield Trinity, 2 eels and 1 try (7 points), Hunslet 1 goal and 1 try (5 points).

div.head: BRADFORD v. SWINTON.
div.p: BRADFORD v. SWINTON.

At Park divenue, before about 6,000 spectators. S ton had to leave out A. Valentine, and substituted Lewis in the three-quarters, and Bradford gave Mosby a'rest. Molyneux dropped a fine goal. The game had scarcely got going again when Eagers scored with an eqUally good drop at the other end. Shortly before the whistle went, Swinton were penalised for off-side, and Eagers from the kick placed his side two points ahead—Eagers dropped another goal, and the close came with Bradford steadily pressing,but unable to cross the line. Result :—Bradford 3 goals (6 points), Swinton 1 goal (2 points). HALIFAX v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.

Played at Halifax, before 5,000 spectators. Half-time score :—Halifax 1 try, Hull Kingston Rovers nil. The Rovers showed up well in the early portion of the second half,•but the home team ultimately assumed the aggressive, and Little struck one of the uprights in taking a shot at goal. Nettleton a little later completed a fine attacking movement and mired. The visitors did not relax their efforts, and a clever passing bout ended in West scoring. Madley's kick at goal was unsuc- cessful. Just before the finish Nettleton cleared the opposition grandly and enabled Joe Riley to score. Wedgwood failed at goal. Result :—Halif ax 3 tries (9 points), Hull Kingston .Rovers 1 try (3 points).

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
WARRINGTON "A" V. WIDNES "A."

This match was decided on the Lower House-lane ground on Saturday, and resulted in Warrington being defeated for the first time this season. In the early stages of the game honours were pretty fairly divided. Warrington were penalized on their quarter-line oppo- site the uprights, but Whelan failed to lower the goal. Warrington began to use their three-quarter line to some advantage and Brooks was nearly over twice in quick succession. Knight missed an easy penalty. Half-time arrived, however, without score. The homesters were unlucky in losing the services of Curtis, whose knee was injured. Play was of a somewhatloose, ! but decidedly brisk order. The Chemicals attacked smartly, and, gaining a penalty for obstructive tactics, Anderson opened the score with a pretty goal. The visitors riltde desperate efforts to score, and Anderson was conspicuous for several smart but risky saves, and in one of these,. when he stopped a certain score, he was iujured. Al orris dribbled through Warrington's lines, and the effort was taken up with a dash that ended in S. Aspey scoring close to the uprights. Result :—Widnes " A," one goal one try (five points) ; Warrington" A." nothing.

div.head: Warrington Church Society Lecture.
div.p: Warrington Church Society Lecture.

"The Bible since the Reformation formed the subject of an interesting lecture which was delivered by the Rev. Chas. Harris at a meeting of the Warring- ton Church Society which was held in St.Jamea's school on Monday evening. During the course of his address Mr. Harris showed by means Of lantern views the various changes which the Bible had under- gone since the time 'if William Tyndale, the first English translator. He pointed out various efforts which had been made to get at the real meaning of the words written by the original writers. Words hid he said, become obsolete, and changed their mean- ing, while there were numerous printers' blunders which had to be corrected. Scholars now knew better how to revise the 'Bible, because there were better facilities for learning, and because several valuable ancient manuscripts had been discovered. Photographs of wood cuts of ancient Bibles were shown on the screen. The lecturer was heartily thanked on the proposition of the Rev. B. Percival, seconded by the Rev. C. A. M. Evans. Mr. H. N. Houghton was thanked for manipulating the lantern, and the Vicar f )r the use of the schools.

LETTERS TO THE _EDITOR.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases sent their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee Of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible, not later than Thursday. L" L. NV. E." writes in continuation of the discussion regarding Parr Hall ser ?ices, which; we closed last week. He desires to explain his last letter and "give the Rev. IL Dunnico full credit for honesty and sincerity of purpose." "If," he says " Fair Play' and others will read my last letter again they will find, I think, that the sum and substance of what I said was to ask Mr. Dunnico to preach on reasonable questions and do a little more practical work."—En. "EL"]

div.head: Mr. A. H. Crostield and the "Observer."
div.p: Mr. A. H. Crostield and the "Observer."

The following letter has been forwarded to the editor of the "Observer" by Mr. A. H. Crosfield. Sir,—l rather think it was Lord Beaconsfield who said, "By your adjectives you shall be judged." If so your correspondent who styles himself " Loyalist " is evidently given to exaggeration. He /eters to my "somewhat ferocious letter." There was nothing ferocious about it. The letter was severe and meant to be so, and I am not surprised that " Loyalist " is smarting under the rebuke he richly deserved. He has made the startling discovery that I know some politicians. It is perfectly true that I have the privelege of knowing Sir John Brunner intimately, and that I am also acquainted with Sir Henry Camp- bell Bannerman, Mr. Lloyd George and Mr. Labouchere. I will make you and your friend "Loyalist" a present of a little further information. Amongst many other people who take an interest in politics I happen to be acquainted with Mr. Asquith and Lord Crewe, and I am still better acquainted with Mr. Winston Churchill, and it is extremely probable that both !Ur. Churchill and Mr. Lloyd George will be speaking in Warrington in the near future. It will be interesting to note the deductions drawn from this by the fertile but erratic brain of your correspondent. Will he see in these facts further evidence of my disqualification for a football match at which the staff of our company invited me to kick-off, or may it dawn upon him that the one thing has as little to do with the other as Tenterden's Steeple with Goodwin Sands. What you call a " crushing reply to my letter is in fact no reply at all, neither are your own lubrica- tions, which I have read with some amusement. You are wise to draw a red herring across our discussion and so seek to divert your readers' attention from the points at issue. People who play at bowls must expect rubbers, and those who are too thick-skinned to give and take the amenities of party warfare had better leave politics alone. - or in ordiaary circumstances do I care one single biassfathink for anonymous attacks such as have recently teen made upon the in your paper. But there is a limit to this kind of thing; and your correspondent oversteps that limit when (in that anxiety to make party capital which he shares equally with yourself) he damages a cause which should appeal to everyone, by imputations which are entirely unjustifiable and contrary to fact. As I said before, it is most chari- table to suppose his first letter was written in ignor- ance : though I repeat you, sir, cannot plead that excuse for publishing it. But may I remind your correspoondent—and yourself—that the fair-minded controversialist, when he finds that either charges or imputations have been made in error, withdraws them. If "Loyalist" does so it will save any further time being spent over this matter. If he does not, then so far as I am concerned this correspondence is equally at an end. If " Loyalist "as he calls himself has anything further to say I would only suggest that he has the courage to put his name to it, because I do not see the slightest excuse or justification for the anonymity under which he shelters himself. Another letter from another anonymous correspond- ent, which you seem to think it good taste to pub- lish, I shall not reply to; except to remind the writer of a Spanish proverb which says that if you stop to throw a stone at every cur that barks at you you will never get to the end of your journey.— Yours B:c.,
A. H. CROSFIELD.
December Bth, 1904.

div.head: ST. HELENS POISONING CASE. – Prisoner Acquitted.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS POISONING CASE. - Prisoner Acquitted.
[Continued front Page 67]
Yesterday's proceedings opened with the address to the jury 137 the prosecuting counsel, Mr. Steel who briefly reviewed the evidence given for the Crown on Thursday.

div.head: DEFENCE.
div.p: THE DEFENCE.

The speech of Mr. Lindon Riley on behalf of the prisoner followed. He submitted that either in actual proof or indubitable inference there was nothing to bring any responsibility for the death of the girl against the mother that could not be brought against the other occupants of the Burndreds' house. Unless the jury could lay their finger upon something which differentiated the prisoner from the other members of the household they were no more entitled to consider her guilty, because by some chapter of happenings she stood in the dock, than they would be in holding the same view towards any other member of the household. Counsel went on to quote from a statement in the Blue Book of the Royal Commission on Arsenical Poisoning. Expert opinions therein expressed read that where a small dose of arsenic had been taken there might be found in the body a larger amount than the daily dose while if large doses had been taken a smaller quantity would be found. The counsel then went on to speak of the affection of the child for its foster parents and their dauglitter. Re- ferring to the insurance Mr. Riley said the policy with the Royal London Company was not an isolated one on the life of deceased. It was a policy which formed part of the insurance of the family group, in which prisoner and hr daughter were included, and was a manifestly reasBnable transaction to be entered into. Counsel concluded with an impassioned appeal on be- half of his client.
THE VERDICT. The jury found a verdict of " Not guilty," and prisoner was discharged.

div.head: MR. R. PIERPOINT M.P. AND RETIREMENT RUMOURS.
div.p: MR. R. PIERPOINT M.P. AND RETIREMENT RUMOURS.
A Contradiction.

The second smoking concert of the season in connec- tion with the Junior Conservative Club was held on Thursday evening. There was a large attendance, Mr. E. Draper presiding. , Mr. H. J. WESTBROOK gave an address on the ques- tion of redistribution, pointing out the inequalities of representation existing at the present time. Mr. R. PIERPOINT said he did not know how the rumour as to his resignation could have originated as he had never intended to retire from the representation of the Borough of Warrington. He intended to stand next time, and what was .more, he intended to win. (Applause.) He must say he had not been asked by the Conservative Association to stand. He was a party man and would abide by their decision, but he hoped thdy would ask him, and if they did so he would stand. (Applause). Mr. PURRPOINT, in respondinr, later to a vote of thanks, said he found Parliamentary work wearisome at times, but he always felt it an honour to represent the town. (Applause.) It would require great things indeed to cause him to retire from the position.

div.head: Christ Church Sale of Work.
div.p: Christ Church Sale of Work.

_ The various parochial funds conneCted with Latch- ford Christ Church have benefitted to the extent of £ll4 as the result of the annual sale of work which was held in the schools on Saturday. As was explained by the Rev. G. C. Briggs, the ordinary parochial organizations absorbed annually £5O of the sum raised at the sale of work. What was raised over and above that sum it was proposed should this year be devoted to two special funds—the fund for the decoration of the church and the endowment fund. Speaking of the endowment fund he remarked that he would like to see it raised from its present figure £lO4 to £l3O or .£2OO. This they hoped to do gradually by setting aside annually a small sum of money. The sale was declared open by Lady Grosvenor, who was heartily thanked for her services on the motion of Mr. John Fairclough seconded by Capt. Waring. The stallholders were : No. 1 stall : Mrs. John Fair- dough and the Misses Smith. No 2: Mrs. G. Dakin and Mrs. Monro. No. 3 • Mrs. Richard Fairclough. No. 4 (toy stall) : Mrs. Venn, Mrs. Jeans, jun., and Miss Atkinson. No. 3 (flower stall) : Mrs. and the Misses Broadbent, and Mrs. Waring. No. 6 (refresh- ment stall): Mrs. James Fairclough, Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. William Pierpoint and Miss Fairclough. Excellent entertainments were given during the after- noon and evening, in which Miss Mabel Fairelough (pianoforte solos), Miss Daunt (song), Mr. W. H. Williams (violin), Miss Dora Fairclough (songs), Miss Rose Briggs (recitations), and the Latchford Quartet Party 'took part.
Edgar WooHord, a carman, who was run over by a motor car at Marlborough Gate, Hyde Park, died on Thursday afternoon. The chauffeur, it is alleged, drove off without effering assistance.

div.head: WORKHOUSE EXTENSION.
div.p: THE WORKHOUSE EXTENSION.
PROTEST BY PROPERTY OWNERS AND RATEPAYERS.
Mr. Hickman's Challenge to Mr. A, J. Jolley.

The indignation w:aich has bem aroused in some quarters by the decision of: the Board of Guardians to erect a new building for the accommodation of aged and infirm inmates was voiced at a public meeting of protest held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-s,reet, on Monday evening under the auspices of the War- rington Property Owners' Association. By a number of speakers, prominent among them being Mr. W. Hickman who has opposed the scheme at the Board meetings, the projected expenditure was strongly de- precated, it being contended that a judicious adminis- tration of oat-relief would be the wisest means of dealing with distress. Mr. Hickman went so far as to throw out a challenge that if Mr. A. J. Jolley, one of the principal advocates of the extension, would resign his s at on the Board, he (Mr. Hickman) would do the same, and meet Mr. Jolley in an electoral con- flict, in order that the ratepayers naght have an oppor- tunity of giving their verdict on the question. The meeting unanimously passed a resolution protesting against the outlay in view of' trade depression. There was a large attendance, Mr. R. ElenshAll (president of the Association) presiding. He was sup- ported by Councillors Skelland, Burton, and Evans. Messrs. J. Lunt, W. Hickman, T. Mw. F. Pendlebury, C. Longshaav, R. Dale, T. Critchley, E. England, A. B. Marsh, NV. H. Stansfield, and J. Hopkins (secretary). In the audience thee were several members of the Board of Guardians, including Mrs.lWilkinson,Mr. T. H. Ash- croft, and Mr. R. Forshaw. Several letters of apology for non-attendance were read, the strongest expression of opinion coming from Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, who wrote I much regret that a business engagement this evening will prevent my attending your meeting, but I shall be represented by Mr. F. J. Carlisle. I think it is LITTLE LESS THAN SCAND.kLOUS that some members of the Board of Guardians should treat with such a lack of courtesy and consideration the representations of the property °vipers and ratepayers. I al w tys understood that those who pail the piper should have some voice in calling the tune, and therefor 3 that the Guardians were elected to serve and represent the ratepayers, the latter being in the position of masters. At election times we see a quantity of literature subscribed "yours respectfully" and "your obedient servant," but it would appear that after the election is over the electors are expected to be non-existent or at least patiently silent. They can pay, but may not say ! I would ask Mr. A. J. Jolley and those who support him to explain how manufac- turers overburdened with rates can afford to pay fair , wages to their workmen, and how can overburdened property owners ever let their houses at fair rents or expend money in repairs and decorations ? It is the workingmen more than any who are suffering the most, as the result of public extravagance, and the remedy lies in their own hands, namely, to eject from office such men as Mr. A. J. Jolley and his supporters. (Applause), 1 Councillor BROUGHwrote that he believed the present difficulty could be overcorneby the reasonable extension of out-door relief and thus obviate the spending of a , large sum of money. Councillor BURTON, who, as events proved was able to attend the meeting, had written characterizing the proposed expenditure as " extravagant and unnecessary." Dr. Fox wrote that he strongly supported the efforts of the Association to postpone for at least a year the extension, and let the ratepayers be in full possession of all the facts before they were committed to the ex- penditure of thousands of pounds. 'Many of the Guardians' themselves were opposed to the scheme being carried out now, and the Guardians had the ways and means to grapple with any temporary pressure which might be experienced until the whole thing was thoroughly investigated and proved to be an actual necessity. "We don't want to be burdened with another white elephant like our too expensive police buildings" added Dr. Fox, and the audience applauded the sentiment. "I am not a mem- ber of the Association," he concluded "but now wish to become one,as your meeting demonstrates that you are going to assert your rights to be heard in the public expenditure of the rates." THE CHAIRMAN'S OPINION.

The CHAIRNIAN pointed out that the watchwords of the Association were "efficiency, economy, and equity." They were no advocates of "cheap and nasty" condi- tions or of low rates under all circumstances. When they struck the note of efficiency it did not mean that heavy expenditure must follow as a mitter of course. Property owners were quite willing to bear their share of rates which were necessary for the good government of the town. The Association sent a very respectful resolution to the Board of Guardians protest- ing against the erection of a new building. They took that course after receiving a considerable amount of information and devoting fair and thorough considera- tionto it. Yet, they knew how the Board treated the resolution. He trusted that the speakers that night would deal with principles and not persons, policies and not men. The Association simply wanted to place the grounds of their attitude before the public. They held that the additional expenditure was unnecessary. that it would be unwise, and that there were other and prob- ably better methods of meeting the present contingency. Their protest represented almost half the rateable value of Warrington, but it did not have the effect of deter- mining the Guirii ins to postpone the erection of the building. The strong feeling in the town, had since the calling of that meeting, been voiced by the Independent Labour Party, and the Association thought they were justified in giving their fellow-ratepayers who were not property omners an opportunity of joing with them in protest. (Applause). THE RESOLUTION.

Mr. T. MAX moved: That this meeting of the pro- perty owners and ratepayers of Warrington offers a respectable protest against any further expenditure for new buildings in connection with the Marrington Workhouse. Consideringithe present depressed state of trade, they are of opinion that it is an inopportune time for any such erpense and trust that the Board of Guardians will reconsider their decision to erect new buildings. He emphasised the point that he did not view the subject in a spirit of animosity towards any particular individual. He was sorry the name of his friend Mr. Jolley had been meationed, as he (Mr. May) had on many occasions worked with him and held him in high regard. He had no doubt Mr. Jolley wanted to do his best for the poor as well as for the general public of Warrington, but those present ventured to differ from him on this important question. It should be borne in mind that the gentlemen who were elected to represent the rate- payers were not the masters of the borough but the servants. The enlargement of the Workhouse at a crisis like the present when trade was falling off was something like question of bricks and mortaragainst empty bellies." Many people who had to spend the rates seemed to be under the impression that they were dealing with a bottomless purse. Most of the money proposed to be spent on the extension would not go to relieve the hunger in the slums of Warrington. A large part of it was going to provide handsome offices and handsome salaries for new officials. (Applause.) Mr. May became somewhat discursive in his remarks, and referred at length to the expenditure on education. Mr. S. BARLOW, who had previously manifested some impatience, said he should strenuously object to Mr. May occupying the time of the meeting unnecessarily. It was absurd. "Let us come to the Workhouse !" he a ted Mr
exclaimed. "W 11

e are a, going to the 'Workhouse" retorL May "if the present rate of expenditure continues." He concluded his speech by stating that the poor of Warrington did not want to go to the Workhouse and they ought not to be driven there. Councillor BARTON seconded. He remarked that in ten years the rents had doubled. The rents had not however, increased to the same extent; in fact he knew property owners who had not demanded an extra penny for rent until the Education rate was imposed He thought it high time that a town like Warrington should try to manage its affairs on 6s. Si. in the Z. (Applause.) He was of the opinion that by a judicious distribution of out-door relief—(applause)—the proper use of the existing Workhouse accommodation and the places we had in the town, we might easily tide over the difficulty. He did not think any ratepayers or pro- perty owners would grudge giving their loyal support to such a course, but to spend £7,000 in extending a great Mansion like we already hal would be reckless and needless. (Applause.) A FIGHTING SPEECH BY MR. HIC;CMAN. MR. JOLLEY CHALLENGED.

In supporting the resolution, Ar. W. Hickman de- livered a vigorous criticism of the Guardians' proposals He pointed out that his appearance on that platform was,due to the facts that he was a heavy ratepayer and a member of the Property Owners' Association and also that he hid been reiuestect by many gentlemen in the town to explain his attitude on the question. (Ap- plause.) There was 'a great deal of misconcep- tion in the minds of the general rate- payers in regard to the scheme, an I he wished to state the matter perfectly clearly. It was not proposed to extend the Workhouse proper and to provide more accon modation for able-bodied paupers but to erect a build big inteemediate in character be- tween the elaborate Infirmary and the House for those unfortunate persons who were not wellenough to be in the House and at he same time were too well to re- main in the Infirmary. Last winter the weather was so bad as to stop a great deal of outdoor employment and thus increase the number of inmates of the House.

• ' Another effect was that many people had to enter the Workhouse Infirmary. The latter building was over- crowded for some time ; there- were perhaps between thirty a.ad. forty patients in excess of the number for which it was registered. Tnat, he admitted was a great inconvenience to the ofiicials and inmates, but he thought there was no Cause for alarm, and subsequent events had proved that he was right. At the present time there was no overcrowding in the Infirmary and he believed there were two beds to spare last Friday. All the time the overcrowding was taking place there was a block of buildings, which was formerly used as the Infirmary, practically empty. (Applause.) He did not consider it necessary to have anew building so long as they had so many empty rooms and beds in the old infirmary. He had never moved that the exten- sion scheme be cancelled but only that it be deferred. He did not say it would nit be necessary at some time to erect a new building, neither did he say that it I would be. Mr. Hickman proceeded to deal with the following arguments advanced by the supporters of the ! schema :

(1) That the old hospital had been condemaed tea years ago by the Local Government Board. (2) That the increase of the population demanded that the new building should be erected. (3) That outdoor relief generated and fostered pauperism. (-I) That the Guardians had not sufficient accommo- dation for the inmates of the Infirmary. :11r. Hickman pointed out that the Local Government. Board transacted their business by letter and not verb- ally. Tney did not convey resolutions from head- quarters by any of their servants. If the old Infirmary had been condemned ten years ago and the Board could not wait another day, as one member affirmed, there would be a-letter to that effect. He had been to the Clerk's office to see if such a letter had been received but the officials had searched in vain for one. There was no communication ei4her condemning the hospital or giving the Guardians the privilege of partially using the premises. It was probably correct to state that the population of the Union had doubled during the last ten years, but extra provision had been made at the Workhouse to cope with the increase. The house and infirmary were registered to accommodate 591 inmates, and as far as he could ascertain the highest number to avail themselves of that accommodation at one time was 57. In an emergency the Board would be allowed to hive twenty inmates above the registered number. (Applause.) If out-relief I generated and fostered pauperism, then the out-relief machinery was very defec- tive. (Applause). It was not, he contended, as perfect as it ought to be and as it might be. It was a remarkable fact that when out- relief in the Warrington Union had been curtailed the number of indoor paupers had increased. As the out-relief recipients had increased,the number of inmates had gone down, with only two exceptions, during all the years for which he had studied statistics. The weak spot in the out-relief system was the lack of regular visitation, scrutiny, and oversight. He did not blame the relievino. officers .because they had already more work than they could do. Another officer was required to visit the people who asked for relief and say whether they were deserving or not. (Applause.) Out-relief if
JUDICIOUSLY AND WISELY ADMINISTERED

would prevent many unfortunate people from breaking 110 their homes. (Applause.) Again alluding to the accommo- dation question, Mr. Hickman said he had inspected the old infirmary,vkich was not being utilized,many times. Every room was clean and sweet, in fact a great deal cleaner than the homes of thousands of workinginen. The estimate of £7,000 for the new building did not include furnishing, drainage, heating and extension of the electrical plant. His estimate of the total cost of the work was not £7,000 but £1.7,001 He based his calculations on the outlay on the new Infirmary which was estimated at £15,000 and ultimately totalled £lO,OOO (Applause). If they required another building at all, it was a workshop Scc., of corrugated iron, and they had workmen in the house who could erect such a structure. Mr. Hickman pointed out that he opposed the erection of the new Infirmary as he was in favour of the removal of the whole of the Workhouse premises to cheap land outside the town. They borrowed the money for the Infirmary at 21 per cent. The Clerk had been asking for the lowest terms for a Lim for the new building, and the best offer was one at 4 per cent. by the Loan Commissioners. If they deferred the scheme for twelve months the state of the money market would probably be more favourable and they would be able to borrow at 31 or 33 per cent. He appealed to his colleagues on the Board to reconsider the question. The Property o.vtnrs' Association seat a courteous letter to the Board, although it was a firm and business-like letter. (Applause.) " Where," con- tinued Mr. Hickman," is the great Goliath of Gath ? Where is the man of mighty intellect, of power and intelligence? I want to
GIVE HIM A CHALLENGE.

I feel as warmly over the spending of the money on one side as he does on the other. If he is willing to back up his own arguments, lam willing to back up mine. lam prepared to resign my seat for No. 1 St. Austin's Ward if he will resign his seat in To.vn Hall Ward—(applause)—and I will fight him with his weaver's beam, and no man shall pay a penny of my, election expenses. I hope he will accept the challenge, and we shall see what we little, puny, weaklings are made of." (Applause.) The Association indeed, would have been a craven-hearted lot of comards to have stood such dictation. There was, hovvever,a bit of grit in them yet, and they were not going to let the matter pass if they could help it. If it was necessary they would
GO TO THE LOCA.L GOV ERSNIENT BOAR.D

_ on the question (Applause). Until the Board had con- vinced them that they had notan'available inch of room in the old infirmary and nowhere to put the sick and dying. and the unfortunate, the Association would not give an and there would be no surrender. (Applause). If that meeting taught some men to be civil to their colleagues and courteous to the electors, it would not have been held in vain. (Applause). The resolution was than put to the meeting and carried unanimously. Councillor SKELLAND moved that a copy of the resolution be sent to the Board of Gaardians, and expressed the hope that it would be more effectual than the previous letter. (Hear, hear.) Mr. H. DA.Lr. seconied. He remarked that if the members of the Association were ignorant they were open to education, and they would be very glad for someone to give them a lift by the way. The proposition was agreed to. A vote of thanks to th, alr nan an I NI-. Hickman concluded the meeting.
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED%

a fair rent, or the same as the farmer paid for the same sort of land, so they would not have increased assess- ments as where the rents were doubled. Fixity of tenure was also most desirable, and, so long as a man cultivated the land fairly, and paid his rent, he should be secure. If they had those conditions he thought they would be better as tenants than as owners, for they would be likely to be bought out as owners." Thin buying-out business is a very serious matter. In a small parish in Norfolk sixty years ago they had a little colony of yeomen, and small owners of land, and they had over one hundred acres of common. But the rich Ahabs coveted poor Naboth's birth-right, and bamboozled, or swindled, or bought them out. The common-land was seized by the manorial lord, and to- day there are only three farmers in the parish. So it comes to pass that rich men buy vast tracts of land,and use them, not for the benefit of the community, but for hunting, and shooting, and their own selfish pleasures. 11l fares the land to hastening ills a prey Where wealth accumulates and men decay. I believe we are on the right track when we are pro- moting such schemes as allotmenta and small holdings for bringing back the labourers to the land. We n)t only find healthy and profitable employment for the cultivators in the village, but we relieve the congestion of the labour market in the towns. Our Co-operative Societies ought to help this movement by buying up suitable estates, and managing them as they do at Dasborough and several other places I have already described. They would find a safeand profitable invest- ment for their money and they would help us to solve some of the most pressing problems of the day.

div.head: MISS ELLA ROYSTON AT THE CO-OPERATIVE HALL.
div.p: MISS ELLA ROYSTON AT THE CO-OPERATIVE HALL.

Miss Ella R)yston's dramatic re.:it,al )1 Cn irs Ity evening attracted an audience which may be re; ariad as quite satisfactory in point of numbers in these days when kindred entertainments seem foredoome 1 to failure with the pablic. But, though Nliss Royston's dramatic and elocutionary gifts are in themselves such as to interest such an audienca,she had the ',,00l fortune to surround herself with quite a company of capable local vocalists who individually and collectively contributed so largely and so well to the evening's entertainment that one sometimes wondered whether the elocutionist V7.1.5,t13 announced, assisted by them, or whether she was not herself rather a supplementary attraction to a con- cert. Nor is there thus implied any disparagement of Miss B3yston's abilities. On the contrary the array of elocutionary gems presented showed that, possessing a marvellous memory, Miss Royston is also gifted with just that dramatic instinct combined with a sense of the humorous, which forms the indispensible equipment of a popular reciter. Noting the great variety of styles characterising the namerous items essayed, it was manifest that, while potent in moving her audience with the deep pathos of A city tale "mad " A first settler's story," Miss Royston's strong point lay rather in the presentment of brighter and lighter incident such as is portrayed in "The miller's maid," "In the usual way" and" A row in the pit." It is perhaps needless to say that Miss Royston's recitals were both well received and highly appreciated by the audience.

The singing of a number of songs and quartets by Miss Arline Harrison, Miss M. W. C..)llin, Mr. J. Babbitt and Mr.J.W. Bibby was meritorious to a degree distinctly above the ordinary level of amateur effort, and once or twice there was quite an outburst of enthusiasm in regard to it. Without depreciating by implication anything done by others it is due to say that Mr. Babbitt carried off the palm. For a touching rendering of "The river of Dart " he was constrained, to respond to a double encore, in doing which his soul- ful interpretation of "Take a pair of sparking eyes" gave still greater delight to the audience. The piano- forte accompaniments were most tastefully played by Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac.

If the County Councils were favourable to the movement they would make a big effort to make this Act a success. If they were un- favourable to it they would do their level best to thwart and hinder it. In 1894 Parliament tried for the fourth time to settle this question and it gave us the Parish Councils Act, which for the first time enabled the County Councils to apply some sort of compulsory powers against unwill- ing landowners, and this has done more to help this movement than all the other Acts of Parliament put together. But this Act is imperfect because it does not give us a cheap and efficient form of compulsion to squeeze land out of hostile owners, like the lady at St. Faith, in Norfolk, who spent a thousand pounds in law rather than allow a single acre of her land to fall into any poor man's bands. If rich landowners of this type can throw money away in litigation and in costly arbitrations, they can make their land so costly that will be of no earthly use for allotmentsand small holdings. _

iNow I have given you the Pailiamentary history of this movement,and have shown you thatyou may as well try to squeeze blood out of a stone, as try to drag any effective reforms of our land Laws from a Parlrament of land-owners. lI.—PRIVATE ENTERPRISE HAS DONE MUCH TO HELP THIS MOVEMENT. I have already described the Salvation Army Farm Colonyat Hadleigh in Essex, and the Co-operative Farm at Roden in Shropshire, and several other interesting experiments some time ago. Let me call yourattention to what has been done in the Eastern counties, and I speak of these with confidence, because I know the men who are the leaders of the movement, and I have seen with my own eyes the kind of work they are doing. I was in Peterborough recently, and I had a chat with I my friend Mr. R. Winfrey, who is one of the pioneers' of a big schieme for providing allotments and small holdings in the eastern countries. He tells me that when he became chairman of the County Council Com- mittee on Allotments for the Spalding district they managed to. secure nearly two thousand acres of land under this latest Act. Then Lord Carrington gave thirty two acres of land to the Council,to be used as an experiment. This land was let out to sixty labourers, and in less than three years they not only paid their rents, but thev'asked for more land. Then Earl Carrington and Mr. Winfrey. and half.- dozen other public spirited gentlemen formed a syndi- cate of their own, and bought one hundred and fifty acres of land, as =experiment in peasant proprietor- ship. The principal and interest are paid bar the cuhi- vators in the form of rent, and at the end ot the term the labourers will be freeholders, and they will own the land they cultivate. . Whenlthe County Council was disinclined to buy'more land, Lord Carrington divided up a farm of two hun- dred and forty acres, placing thirty or forty men,raainly agricultural labourers, upon it. There were about eighty acres of land attached which the labourers did not at first see their way to use, as they had not capital for stock, so it was let to a butcher. But before the end of three years the men said they were prepared to take the grass land too, and now they have between sixty and seventy head of stock belonging to the men. Two years later another farm became vacant, and was divided up, so that in one district, besides the County Council farm, they had 700 acres of Lord Carrington s land on a twenty-one year's lease. They had a colony of two hundred and ten prosperous men, who were agricultural labourers ten years ago. One of these men, who was pereonally known to Mr. Winfrey, was a farm labourer twenty years ago. He was one of thd fortunate few who shared in the first allotments, and he has been specially lucky in his under- takings, for to-day he has nearly forty acres of land,and he is saving one hundred pounds.a year. When I talk about these successes I often find men saying that Lincolnshire is well adapted for small hold- ings, but men could not succeed so well in other counties. Mr. Winfrey says that he and seven other gentlemen purchased an estate in Norfolk in 1900, con- sisting of three farms, comprising 340 acres of land, as an experiment. The labourers are perfectly satisfied with their lots, and they are able to pay their rents promptly and in full. In four years, out of a rental of nearly , two thousand pounds, only six pounds remains unpaid. It is interesting to know what sort of men these are who succeed on the land, and I cannot do better than give you Mr. Winfrey's opinions in his own words. He says: "It is no use putting Suffolk men on Lincolnshire land; you must have men who under- stand the cultivation of their own soil, and the local conditions that affect their interests. And you,. must not put a number of men on the land who have failed as labourers, or in any otheri vvay of life, for if a man is a failure at one thing, he is likely to fail at another. They wanted land that was adapted for small holdings. and that could be cultivated in wet or dry seasons, and that could be ploughed with one horse, or not more Oen twe. It was most important that they should have

div.head: " BELPHEGOR." ---- Successful Dramatic Performances.
div.p: " BELPHEGOR." ---- Successful Dramatic Performances.

So much has been written in praise of local charitable institutions that it is unnecessary here, to more than briefly commend the very deserving venture of the drama- tic performances given an the Parr Hall this week by the members of the St. Mary's Dramatic Society, in aid of the District Nursing Association. The institution is doing an extremely useful work in the town and being dependent altogether upon voluntary contributions, the annual addition which the St. Mary's amateurs make to its funds is particularly acceptable. Apart, however, from the object of the production, the merit of the performances has been sufficient to secure a full measure of patronage. The play selected for presentation," Belphegor," which was chosen by the popular vote of the patrons of the society, is one of the oldfashioned type, but it still appeals to the audience, though the plot as not a particularly strong one. The action of the drama is centred rounda strolling player and his wife who while living together in poverty, are separated as the result of the machinations of the villain, only to be re-united and received into the lap of luxury in the last act,and permitted to occupy the high position in society which was theirs by right of birth. Naturally in such a composition,incidents occur which require specially careful, not to say delicate, treatment in order to produce the desired effect. Unfortunately in the production this week, while the leading charac- ters worked upon and enlisted the sympathies of their auditors, the efforts of several impersonators of'minor characters occasionally had a contrary result, and the curtain was rmag down with the audience hesitating between laughter and tears. Another point which re- quired greater attention was the grouping of the com- pany, which on Wednesday night gave one the impres- 1 ston that effectiveness from a spectacular point of view had not been sufficiently considered. On the whole, I however, the production was a meritorious one, reflect- ing credit upon the Society's members, and affording ontertainment to a considerable audience each evening. Dealing with the characters individually, Mr. W. Kilduff stood out prominently as the ore to whom the most difficult part had been allotted. In the title role his acting throughout showed a careful study and appreciation of the spirit of the part he had to portray. Constantly called upon to give expression to varying moods, his interpretation of the idea of the author was very creditable indeed. If anything could be advanded which would detract from the merit of his acting it could only be that at times his pronunciation was not altogether perfect. As the wife of Belphegor, Miss 1 Nora Fleming had also a part which embraced many : trying situations and her spirited acting was deserving of 1 high praise,though occasionally she was,perhaps, a little 1 too emotional. Mr. S. Ryan as the villain Lavarennes i was well placed and filled the part admirably. He dis- 1 played no mean ability in the earlier stages of the , drama, when he, after persistent efforts to get the heroine into his power, induced her to leave her hus- 1 band under the pretext of saving the life of her dying , child. While he infused plenty of vigour into the : part he by no means exaggerated the black propensities, accredited Laverennes by the writer of the drama. Mr. I A. Kilduff was largely zesponsible for the humor us element in the piece and well fulfilled his office,thot h ; enunciation is a point which he also might pay greal er attention to. Mr. C. J. Newton seldom fails to give a good account of himself, and as the Duke de Montbazon he achieted a ' distinct success. His "Nephew" Mr. John Newns had to portray a somewhat affected and effeminate aristocrat and took the part almost to perfection, though in certain scenes his actions lacked the necessary freedom. Miss Delia Gleeson infused plenty of life into her acting, in the ! role of "Zephyrina Petitpas," especially in the scene in which she is introduced to the Duke de Montbazon, when she portrayed the light-hearted coquette in a , finished manner. 1

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. (By 7-)valist.",
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. (By 7-)valist.",

Warrington were winners again on Saturday, but they gave such a poor display of football that the spectators were anything but pleased. Perhaps it is hardly fair to blame the home club, however. I forecasted the style of game likely to ensue, in my notes of last week, and the forecast was fully borne out. Widnes do not go in for open tactics, but attempt rather to restrict the combination of their opponents to harmless limits. In plain language Widnes are a team of spoilers, and they would, in my view, win more matches if they adopted more scientific methods. Preventing the other side from scoring does not result in many pints or much glory, and the sooner the "Chemicals " realise that to go in for scoring themselves is a much more effective and sportsmanlike game, the better it will be for them and football generally.

The scoring on Saturday was practically restricted to the one try which Fish and Di Davies engineered between them, though Warrington notched a trio of penalty goals in addition and finished up nine points ahead. In any case Widnes w uld probably have lost, because they are an inferior hide, but if they had played an open game the result/would certainly have been better from the spectators' point of view Nowadays, footballers are so carefully selected and highly trained that the crowd has a right to expect U decent exposition of the game. Taken as a whole Widnes are a better fifteen than their record would suggest, and they possess men capable of superior work if they would only employ their energies in the right direction. There is both strength and pace in the Widnes .team, but combination sadly requires cultivating.

So far this season the Warrington men have not shown either good or consistent form. They have an excellent side, but the backs do not seem to have got going at all well. Isherwood and Dickenspn seem to have—temporarily only I hope—lost the art of centre play, though the former is certainly showing improved form. For such famous exponents, however, the Warrington threequarters as a whole are doing neither themselves nor the club credit. Perhaps they will do as they have done before—come with a rush. If it happens to-day at Salford there will be some Warringtonians on the spot ready to rejoice.

For once in a way Warrington were able on Satur- day to place their full strength in the field, HDckenhall and Boardman b)th being fit ag tin, hut they finished up a man short,as Dickenson was badly kicked in the last few minutes of the game. They may therefore have to take ths field to-day minus the right centre, but as Dickenson has not so far shown anything; like his best form the team may be no worse off, and the rest may do the player himself some good.

There was far too much keenness imported into last Saturday's contest. The Widnesians became par- ticularly fierce when Warrington got a goal. and a try ahead, and some of the " scrums " were like "tupping" matches. Consequently the ball seldom travelled far beyond the " Scrum " and open play was at a dis- c-mint. The forward argument was very even, and neither side could claim much advantage here though Warrington were the heavier lot. At half back Hockenhall and Davies were ahead of the Widnes pair, for whom Lally spoiled an otherwise good display by his faulty throw-in. There was rather more cohesion au.ong th 9 home threequarters than among their opponents and they were as a rule the more dangerous guar- tete, but it was really a game in which defence was more prominent than attack. The two full backs both distinguished themselves, and it was a source of pleasure to the home crowd to see Hallam showing much of his old brilliance in clearing.

The match had an important bearing both in the Northern ,League and the South-West Lancashire League. Warrington now occupy third place in the former, having in the course of a fortnight paped Leeds, Wigan, and Hunslet in the race. They possess one of the best point averages in the competition, no other clubkaving so few points scored against them. If they can keep up their average they should finish very near the head of the table.
The South-West Lancashire League table up-to-date is as follows :

Warrington still possess a clear lead in the above, but they have yet to play four matches away, and must not get over-confident. Their only serious opponents so far are Leigh, from whom I do not fear much. Their hopes are likely to be dashed on the last day of the year, when the return game is played at Wilderspool.

There is a great deal of interest being taken in to day's visit to Salford. Last season Warrington astonished the natives of Weaste by a fine back 'dis- play and won by 11 points to 3, Fish notching a couple of brilliant tries. The respective form of the two clubs points to Warrington repeating the dose, and a large crowd is sure to follow them. It will be a hard fight, but Warrington should prove their superiority before the close. They have a stronger fifteen than on the last occasion, while the Reds are probably weaker. Their defeat at Broughton by 20 points to 5 shows what smart combination can do, and I am hoping to see the Warrington backs at their best.

Salford have made a rather remarkable alteration in their team, the redoubtable Lomas being placed on the , wing, probably with the idea of watching Fish. The change should be to Warrington's advantage, for the burly Cumberland man ought to be easier to keep under control when near the touch-line, and Fish can !always keep his end up. The opposite wing should prove rather easy prey to Harris and Co., whom I hope •to see getting more opportunities.

I The Salford selection is as follows :—W. Lambert, ' full back; J. Lomas (captain), W. Thomas, R. Richards, and G-. Baker, three-quarter backs; D. Preston and J. Maddocks, half backs; P. Tunney, J. Rhapps, T. Lewis, H. Buckler, A. Buckler, W. Brown, H. Rees, and A. Foster, forwards. R. Shaw, reserve.
The Warrington team will be the same as last week with the exception that Brooks has been selected to fill the vacancy at centre caused by Dickenson's in- jury.

The "A " team sustained their first reverse at Widnes, where the home side won by 5 points to nil after a very keen. struggle. J. Davies', absence made a considerable difference to the , Warrington team, which is still well in the running for the combination championship being bracketed first with Wigan " A " A god game should result from the meeting with Salford "A "at Wilderspool to-day.

Hockey. [BY R.G P.] Much to the disgust of the Stockton Heath eleven, the match at Western was cancelled owing to the ground being unfit. This is the second week in succession that the club has been kept out of the field, owing to the weather.

However, the Second Eleven managed to fulfil their engagement with Western 2nd at Grappenhall-road, and beat the visitors by no less than 5-0. The goals for the home side were scored by W. Richardson, 3; W. Howard, 1; W. Longdin, 1.

This afternoon New Brighton Wanderers will be opposed, and the following teams have been chosen to represent Stockton Heath :—First (away), R. G. Pier point, goal; E. Pierpoint and E. E. Woods, backs; L. Fairclough, Eric Fairclough, and J. Richardsdn, halves; C. H. Bond, S. Baxter, R. Pierpoint, W. Richardson, and R. Fairclough, forwards. Referee, Mr. Bellamy. div.head: FREE TRADE SUPPORTED. Another Social Service League Debate.
div.p: FREE TRADE SUPPORTED. Another Social Service League Debate.

"That this meeting declares its enthusiastic adher- ence to the principles of Free Trade and its belief that only through the fuller application of those principles can the industry and commerce of our country be firmly established and the wellbeing of the people secured." Such was the resolution passed almost unanimously at.the weekly debate in connection with the Social Service League held in Golborne-street schoolroom on Thursday evening. A weaker case for Protection was probably never placed before a meeting, and it was little wonder that the verdict was overwhelmingly in favour of the maintenance of Free Trade. The debate was an exceedingly interesting one, and was evidence that the League is serving a useful educational purpose. The Rev. H. Dunnico presided over a good attendance. The tnoving of the Free Trade resolution was entrust- ed to Mr. Edmund Osborne who declared that he be- lieved in Free Trade because it was morally and politi- cally right, and he objected to Protection because it was ethically and economically unsound. Since we had had Free Trade, he pointed out,our national wealth had enormously increased and in the distribution of that wealth the lot of the very poor had steadily im- proved. The wages of the labouring classes in this country were better, and their general standard of com- fort higher than those of similar classes in any country in Europe. Quoting figures, Mr. Osborne emphasised the fact that the percentage of unemployed as wall as the ratio of pauperism had decreased under Free tirade.. The British working nan was 50 per cent better off thaa th 3 Germaa workingman. As I instancing the effects of Protective measures Mr. Osborne pointed out how an increased price of sugar had followed the Sugar Convention and not only was it affecting the pocket of the workingman but it was also ruining the industries which depended largely upon the Sugar supply. In seconding, Mr. WYNNEJONES said Mr. Chamberlain. told them that our trade was going to the dogs. Yet three years ago Mr. Chamberlain stated we were supreme commercially and industrially over all the nations of the world. Ef both his statements were right it must be a case of" galloping consumption.' Our foreign trade was actually the best in the world, and we did it at a bigger profit than America or Ger- many. He did not believe the loyalty and affection of our colonies were to be purchased with money. By restricting the market in sugar the recent Convention made it possible for a "corner "to be organized, and the price of the commodity was raised. What was the object of those who spent great sums on the Tariff Reform League and the purchasing of independent newspapers? The system was really a vast pool into which rich men were putting their money in the hope that they would get hundreds per cent, in return. While not defending "Protection pure and simple" Mr. HA.WTHORNE said he was a supporter of fair trade. If other countries would not give us Free Trade it was not fair that we should give Free Trade to all and sundry. He granted that the convention had something to do with the advance in the price of sugar, but the shortage of crops had far more effect. . Mr. JACKSON narrated some of his own experiences of the conditions under Protection, and advised his hearers not to attempt to revert to those days. Mr. E. LLOYD JONES contended that a tax on raw' material would increase the cost of everything we used. Trade generally was not bad. It was only in particular instances that depression was being experienced. The ' returns for the past month showed that in every department we had an increase of trade as compared with November, 1903. Mr. H. P. HUGHES, who is well-known as a Protec- tionist, did not attempt to shatter the arguments of the Free Trade speakers. Lie expressed regret that the question had been made a political one. After devotiag a considerable time to explain the collapse of a fustian industry in which he was formerly engaged, Mr. Hughes pointed out that cotton was responsible for a good proportion of our export trade, and it was largely the product of female labour. Out of our 200,000 seamen, 70,000 were foreigners, and the pro- portion was growing year by year. Mr. E. PLDTSTON took Mr. Hughes to task rather warmly for having, as he termed it" wasted time." The workingmen, he declared were not going to be mis- led by Mr. Chamberlain. Before they would agree to his proposals an increased wage must be assured in order to meet the additional cost of bread.

Dealing with the decline in the fustian industry, Mr. Osborne emphasised the fact that it was due to the change of fashion. The Rev. EL DosNrco pointed out that we were par: ing more to enter Canada than we were to any other European country. Canada only did one quarter of her trade with us but we had to pay for the whole up-keep of the navy which protected the empire. We supplied 66 per cent of the total imports of India. Taking our colonies, we only did 12 per cent of our total trade with them and 83 per cent with other nations. We were asked to jeopardise the 88 .per cent for the sake of benefitting the people who simply did 12 per cent. Our export trade to-day was twice as much per head as the German and six times as much per head as the United States export trade. The resolution was carried by 39 votes to 2.

THE IRON TRADE. Fate of the Midland Wages Board. An important meeting is to be held on Nlonday,which will settle the fate, for thetime being, of the Midland Wages Board, which since the seventies has settled dis- putes and regulated wages of ironworkers in South Wales, Shropshire, And South Staffordshire. The opera- tives, it will beremembered. gave notice to discontinue the sliding scale, and at the same time let it be known that they wanted a more representative body. At Monday's meeting a resolution is to be submitted providing for the continuance of the Board's functions, but at present the feeling is that it is not at all safe to jump to the conclusion that things will go on as before.. In the event of a revision of the Board's functions, one of the first matters needing attention would be the provision ata new sliding scale to take the place of the one just abolished. This would be a lengthy matter, probably involving the taking of " ascertainments" for a period of twelve months. In the meantime the men's wages would be regulated by the process which has in reality been in operation for the last two years; that is to say, they would be paid at the same rate as that prevailing in the North of England, with 6d. per ton added.

VOLUNTEER PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.' New Quarters Opened. An additional inducement for young men to identify themselves with the local volunteer battalion, is being held out by the provision which has recently been made for the social entertainment of those who locally have joined this branch of our auxiliary forces. The depar- tures which have been made in this direction would not have been possible but for the erection at the rear of the old Drill Hall of a large building, mainly to be devoted to this object. In this building rooms have beengset apart for the use of privates and corporals and as officer and sergeants' messes already existed all grades of the service are now furnished with means which will permit of conviviality. In addition a large concert hall has been provided in which entertainments arranged by the men can be periodically held, and altogether nothing has been omitted which will tend to an improvement in the social side of the volunteering so far as Warrington is concerned. The recent addition to the volunteer quarters were used for the first time on Monday evening, when the annual prize distribution took place. There was a good muster of the men and a full attendance of officers and in addition there were present the Mayor, Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P., Dr. Marken, the Rev. W. Bracecamp, the Rev. Canon Willis, Major Roome Colonel Ridgway, and Messrs. A. IL Crosfield, W. H. Bleckley, R. T. Fairclough, John Fairclough, Segar Owen, F. Monks, H. Roberts, J. Monro and J. White. Colonel EDELSTEN, who presided, remarked that that Alight a slightly new departure was being made in the history of the corps. The officers and sergeants of the battalion had had their mess rooms for a long time and now rooms had been provided which would to a certain extent extend to the corporals and privates those advantages I prdviously and exclusively enjoyed by the officers and sergeants. (Applause). The new building would also afford military: advantages by permitting of the concen- tration of their military effects which, from a military point of view was most important. The advantages which the corporals-and privates would derive from the new rooms would rest entirely with themselves. They would be managed by an executive committee consist- ing of Major Fairclough, Captain Bundock. Rev. W. Bracecamp and Quarter Master Sergeant Potter, and a general committee consisting of four officers, two sergeants, two corporals, and two privates to be elected directly by the rank which they represented. In the mess rooms canteens would be established, and it was proposed that the profits arising from the canteens should be devoted to the arranging of pleasurable entertainments for the men. Altogether, he thought, they had something which would tend to their advantage, and which would make volun- teering in Warrington more pleasurable than it had been A hitherto. Colonel J. Thc Art of Book-keeping.—Lord Rosebery who is always a delightful talker on the subject of books, said the other day, some hard things about people who borrow books and fail to return them. It is thought that in this respect women are greater sinners than men, but it is always folly to lend a book without keep- ing a memorandum of the circumstance, whoever the borrower may be. It is still better never to lend any books at all, and this is the only way to do with certain people who make a habit of borrowing books and never intend to return them. Lord Rosebery would call them "book thieves," but there are others who fall into the same failing with the best intentions in the world. Some book borrowed at an odd moment, is forgotten, and 4ould never be returned unless its owner kept a note of its whereabouts; and asked for it back. ,

Toe problem is always a trouble- some one for municipalities, which, while they grow continually, take no account of the probabty overburdened drainage system. In Warrington the sewers are like many other things,—relics of the past—and while they sufficed admirably for the town twenty years ago they are rapidly becom- ing incapable of performing the duties required of them. In Orford :district the congestion is serious and a scheme has been adopted whereby it is hoped to remove the difficulty. This scheme will involve a capital outlay of £:2,000, but only the small annual charge of £5O. Since the Conncil sanctioned the scheme, however, the Rural District Council has 'taken steps to join in with the Corporation. The outlying districts at the same end of the town are similarly in need of extended sewering, so that it is likely the existing scheme will have to be enlarged. The Rural authorities will, of c)urse, bear their share of the expense, but it seems to us that this development may force upon the Cor- poration the necessity of going further than they intended. Practically the whole town needs re- sewering, but it is to be hoped the evil and expensive day for such an outlay may be warded off for some time to come. As a set-off to the alarming expenditure men- tioned above it is satisfactory to learn that one department of the Corporation is entitled to congratulate itself. Coacentrated manure is going strongly, and the Sanitay Committee announce with gusto that they are able to reduce the price and improve the quality. This is good news for the consumers. Pity it is that the users of Corporation gas are not in as happy a position. The manure seems to be better than the gas—for its own particular purpose of course. But it is a little curious that of all the commodities the Corporation deals in—water, gas, electricity, etc.— concentrated manure is the only one which shows as profit and gives satisfaction at the same time.

The General Purposes Committee had resolved to ; defer the consideration of the purchase of a site for a I new school in Orford Ward, but the Mayor said the ' decision would appear on the agenda for the next meet- ! ing. The inspector had informed him distinctly that jno other site but the one recommended would suit the Local Government Board.
