The minutes were approved. THE ST. HELENS POISONING CASE. WOMAN CHARGED WITH MURDER. PRISONER ACQUITTED. Ellen Burndred, aged 49, was placed on her trial at , Liverpool Assizes on Thursday, before Mr. Justice Phillimore, on a charge of having murdered Sarah Ann Jones at St. Helens on the 7th August. Mr. A. G. Steel, K.C. and Mr. F. Smith prosecuted, and Mr. H. Lindon Riley and Mr. Robert Segar were counsel for the defence. SPEECH FOR THE PROSECUTION. Mr. Steel said Jones, at the age of six years, was de- serted by her father in 1895, and was in consequence taken to the Whiston Workhouse, near St. Helens. In 1 1901 she was adopted by the prisoner, who said she I wanted her for a companion for her daughter, Sophia, then a girl of 14 or 15. With thei exception of a few weeks the deceased child had lived with the Burndreds from that time until the 7th August last,when she died. It was impoctant to remember that shortly after the girl went to reside with the Burndreds she was insured in the Royal London Friendly Society for £2O, the premium being something like 2d. a week. In May or June of this year, Mr. Steel continued the prisoner visited certain glassworks in St. Helens and asked a man there to supply her with a quantity of arsenic, which she required fora limewash, or something of that kind. This man refused to comply with the request. On the 25th July the dinner in the Burndred's house was prepared by the prisoner; it consisted of cold meat, cold cabbage, green peas, and potatoes After the meal had been eaten the young man to whom the prisoner's daughter Sophia was engaged and the girl Jones became ill with pains in the stomach, &c. The young man got better, but the girl became worse on the 26th July. On the 29th July Dr. Bellew, a local practitioner, came to the conclusion that the girl's symptoms pointed to gastritis, but the jury would be told that the symptoms of gastritis and arsenical poisoning werealike. He (Mr. Steel) did not think there could be the slightest doubt that the cause of death was arsenical poisoning. The only motive which the prose- cution alleged in that case was that the prisoner was nit doubtedly hard up for money. Her husband was out of work; she had no business of her own, and, although the amounts involved were small, she was in fact being pressed by several creditors, while there was ajudge- ment out against her for £1 12s. 6d. On the 20th August—the day before the body was exhumed —an inspector informed the Burndreds that a post-mortem examination of the body was to be made. On the 21st August the prisoner was seen by a witness in the case near a pond in the district. She threw something into the pond, and shortly afterwards the witness saw her struggling in the pond. The wit- ness rushed to the prisoner's assistance, hnd with some trouble released her from the situation in which she was placed. In fairness to the prisoner it should be stated that her house had been diligently searched by ' the police, but no arsenic or any other poison was found. WITNESSES FOR THE CROWN. Relieving officers and an insurance agent were the first witnesses. John Heyes, a clerk in the yard office of Messrs. Pilkington's glassworks, gave evidence in reference to the prisoner having asked him to supply her with arsenic, which he refused to do. He did not hear her say that she intended to use the arsenic in a house which was infested with vermin. John Henry M'lntegart, the young man engaged to Sophia Burndred, said that when Jones was ill she expressed a desire to sleep with Mrs Burndred, whom she always called mother. All the Burndreds seemed genuinely attached to the girl, and the first night after the girl had gone back to the workhouse Mrs. Burndred wanted her back, saying her absence had affected her sleep. After the dinner on the 25th July all the family were ill, and Mrs. Burndred 's attack was so acute that she had to get medicine from the doctor. They all recovered with the exception cf the deceased. Mr. Riley : From first to last was there any secret treatment—any exclusion of friends or neighbours or household from the girl Jones? Not the slightest. Continuing, the witniss said he had never seen the slightest sign of potrerty about the house. Mr. Burndred had told him that while he was at home suffer- ing from the effects of an accident at Messrs. Pilking- ton's works he was in receipt of more money by way of workmen's compensation and allowances from friendly societies than if he had been in full work. Sophia Burndred, daughter of the prisoner, gave evidence that about £2O was spent on the funeral. Until the Thursday before the Sunday on which she died the girl had exactly the same food as the rest of , the family. Then by the doctor's instructions, she was given barley and water. When she died the prisoner was prostrated with grief. Thomas Wilson, a labourer, describing the pond inci- dent, said that after he had rescued the woman, he asked her what she had thrown into the water, and she said it was her slipper. Asked also why she had jumped into the water, she replied "Trouble." Evidence was also given as to a pair of slippers having been found in the pond. ARSENIC IN THE BODY. Mr. Herbert Edward Davies, analyst, said the arsenic was pretty evenly disseminated over the organs of the , body. He should imagine that the arsenic had been ,1 taken in more than one dose,but it was impossible to be positive as to this. There was not a trace of arsenic in the medicines and ointments which were sent to him for analysis. In cross-examination by Mr. Riley, the Iwitness said there were possibilities although they were very remote, of foodstuffs becoming contaminated with arsenic. By the Judge: The arsenic, if taken in one dose in the cabbage on the Monday week before the child's death, would, judging by the residuum he found in the body, have caused death long before the 7th Of August. Dr. Unsworth endorsed this view. Dr. Bellew and Dr. Unsworth stated that in their opinion arsenical poisoning was the cause of death. • Simultaneously with the publication of Professor Haeckel's new work, " The Wonders of Life," Messrs.
